And al-Fattal related to me al-Tanwir fi Ma'ani al-Tafsir and the Kitab Rawdat al-Wa'izin wa-Basirat al-Mutta'izin; and al-Tabrisi announced to me the Majma' al-Bayan li-'Ulum al-Qur'an and the Kitab I'lam al-Wara bi-A'lam al-Huda; and Abu al-Futuh granted me licence to relate Rawd al-Jinan wa-Ruh al-Jinan fi Tafsir al-Qur'an; and Abu al-Hasan al-Bayhaqi handed over to me the Hilyat al-Ashraf; and al-Amidi gave me leave to relate the Ghurar al-Hikam; and I found in the hand of Abu Talib al-Tabrisi his book al-Ihtijaj. Such things are too many to enumerate, and there is no need to

Al-Shaykh Muntajab al-Din said: Al-Sayyid 'Imad al-Din Abu al-Samsam Dhu al-Fiqar b. Muhammad b. Ma'bad al-Hasani al-Marwazi, learned and religious; he relates from the most eminent Sayyid al-Murtada 'Alam al-Huda Abu al-Qasim 'Ali b. al-Husayn al-Musawi, and from al-Shaykh al-Muwaffaq Abu Ja'far Muhammad b. al-Hasan, may God sanctify their spirits. I met him, and he was a hundred and fifteen years old.
In Amal al-Amil: He was learned and devout, one of the students of al-Sayyid al-Murtada and al-Sayyid al-Radi.

70.text: mentioning them, given their agreement upon it. And this is but a part of a whole; nor am I — God the Exalted knows — anything but one who confesses incapacity and shortcoming, as Abu al-Jawa'iz said:
I have related, and yet of the narration I have related nothing — and how, when I have reached no end?
Deeds have ends at which they finish, however long they run; but knowledge has no end.

In this book I have aimed at confining myself to the texts of the reports, and have turned aside from lengthiness and multiplication, from argument drawn from surface meanings and from inference upon their purport. And I have dropped their chains because of their fame, and because I have pointed to their transmitters, their routes, and the books from which they were extracted — so that they may thereby pass out of the category of chainless reports and be joined to the class of those with full chains.

It may be that reports overlap one another, and the place of need is abridged from them, or we choose what is fewer in wording; or a report comes as a rarity from remote sources, or arrives in a repellent form standing in need of interpretation. Among them is what the Qur'an accords with; among them what a great many have related, until it became necessary knowledge binding them to act by it; among them what its traces have preserved, whether by sight or by hearing; and among them what the poets and the versifiers have uttered, on account of its currency. Thus the virtues of the People of the House, peace be upon them, became manifest by the consensus of those who agree with them — and their consensus is a proof, as has been stated in more than one place — and became widely known upon the tongues of those who differ from them, by way of compulsion, for they are unable to deny what God has caused their own transmitters to utter and has set running upon the mouths of those they hold trustworthy, together with the Shi'a's mass transmission of it. That is a breaking of custom, and an admonition for whoever takes heed. So the Shi'a came to be granted success in what they transmitted, and were made at ease; and the Nasiba came to be disappointed in what they carried, and were made a mockery — since this party transmits what is a proof for it in its religion, while that party carries what is a proof for its adversary and not for itself. And this is sufficient for one who "gives ear while he is a witness"; and "this indeed is the manifest trial"; and a reminder for those who remember, and a kindness from God the Exalted to the worlds.
This is the end of what we have transmitted from al-Manaqib.

And let us mention what we found at the opening of the Tafsir of the Imam al-'Askari, God's blessings be upon him. The Shaykh Abu al-Fadl Shadhan b. Jibra'il b. Isma'il al-Qummi — may God perpetuate his support — said: There related to us al-Sayyid Muhammad b. Sharahatak (1) al-Hasani al-Jurjani, from al-Sayyid Abu Ja'far

In the Tafsir: Sarahanak al-Hasani al-Jurjani. Further, it appears that Muhtadi is a corruption of Mahdi — he being, as comes below from al-Ihtijaj, Mahdi b. al-'Abid Abu al-Harb al-Husayni al-Mar'ashi. Al-Muhaqqiq al-Wahid, may God have mercy on him, counted him in the Ta'liqa among the eminent men of the community and among the masters of licence.

71.text: Muhtadi b. Harith al-Husayni al-Mar'ashi, from the Shaykh al-Saduq Abu 'Abd Allah Ja'far b. Muhammad al-Duristi, from his father, from the Shaykh, the jurist, Abu Ja'far Muhammad b. 'Ali b. Babawayh al-Qummi, may God the Exalted have mercy on him. He said: There informed us Abu al-Hasan Muhammad b. al-Qasim al-Astarabadi the preacher, may God the Exalted have mercy on him. He said: There related to me Abu Ya'qub Yusuf b. Muhammad b. Ziyad and Abu al-Hasan 'Ali b. Muhammad b. Sayyar (1) — and the two of them were of the Imami Shi'a — who said: Our fathers were Imamis, and the Zaydis were the dominant party at Astarabad. That was under the rule of al-Hasan b. Zayd al-'Alawi, styled the Summoner to the Truth, the Imam of the Zaydis (2); and he listened much to them, and would kill people upon their informing. So we feared for ourselves on their account, and went out with our households to the presence of the Imam al-Hasan b. 'Ali b. Muhammad, the father of the Qa'im, peace be upon him. We lodged our families in one of the caravanserais (3), then sought leave to enter upon the Imam al-Hasan b. 'Ali, peace be upon them both. When he saw us he said: Welcome to those who take refuge with us, who seek shelter in our care (4). God has accepted your striving, and made secure your fright (5), and sufficed you against your enemies. So return, secure as to yourselves and as to your properties. We marvelled at his saying that to us, though we did not doubt his truthfulness in what he said. So we said: What do you command us to do, O Imam, until we come to be there? And how are we to enter that town from which we fled, while the sultan of the town seeks us urgently (6) and his threat against us is severe? He said: Leave behind these two sons of yours, that I may impart to them the knowledge by which God the Exalted will ennoble them. Then pay no regard to the informers, nor to the threat of the one informed to; for God the Exalted will crush the informers (7) and drive them to seek your intercession for them with the very one from whom you fled. Abu Ya'qub and Abu al-Hasan said: So the two of them did as he commanded, and departed, and left us there. And we would go back and forth
His biography has already been given in the second introduction.

Ibn al-Nadim gave his entry in his Fihrist thus: al-Hasan b. Zayd b. Muhammad b. Isma'il b. al-Hasan b. Zayd b. al-Hasan b. 'Ali, peace be upon them both, styled the Summoner to the Truth. He appeared in Tabaristan in the year 250 and died there, ruling over it, in the year 270.
Al-khan: the lodging place of travellers, also called a funduq. Plural: khanat.
Al-kanaf: the side; and a bird's kanaf are its two wings.
Qasama a man: destroyed him. And al-si'aya: talebearing and informing.

72.text: to him, and he would meet us with the kindness of fathers and of close kin. One day he said to us: When there comes to you the news of God Almighty's sufficing your fathers, and His disgracing their enemies, and the truth of my promise to them, I shall make it part of my thanks to God Almighty that I impart to you the commentary of the Qur'an, comprising some of the reports of the family of Muhammad, peace be upon them, so that your standing may thereby be magnified. He said: So we rejoiced, and said: O son of the Messenger of God, shall we then come upon all the sciences of the Qur'an and its meanings? He said: By no means. Al-Sadiq, peace be upon him, taught some of his companions what I intend to teach you, and he rejoiced at that and said: O son of the Messenger of God, I have gathered the whole science of the Qur'an. He said: You have gathered much good and been given ample excellence; yet with all that, it is the least little of the parts of the science of the Qur'an. God Almighty says: "Say: if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, though we brought the like of it for replenishment" (1); and He says: "And if all the trees in the earth were pens, and the sea, with seven seas after it to replenish it, the words of God would not be exhausted" (2). And this is the science of the Qur'an and its meanings, and the wonders deposited in it. How much, then, do you reckon the measure of what you have taken of all this to be? Yet the measure you have taken — God has favoured you by it over everyone who does not know as you know, nor understand as you understand. They said: We did not leave his presence before there came to us a courier (3) sent from our fathers with a letter, mentioning in it that al-Hasan b. Zayd al-'Alawi had killed a man upon the informing of those Zaydis and confiscated his property. Then letters came from the districts and the regions, bearing the hands of the Zaydis, with severe reproach and great rebuke, mentioning in them that the man killed was the most excellent Zaydi on the face of the earth, and that the informers had aimed at him for his excellence and his wealth. So he was grateful to them, and ordered their noses and their ears cut off; and some of them were indeed so mutilated, and others fled. And the 'Alawi repented and asked forgiveness and gave great sums in charity, after returning the property of that slain man to his heirs, and offered them many times over the blood-money of their slain kinsman, and asked them to absolve him. They said: As for the blood-money, we absolve you of it; but as for the blood, that is not ours — it belongs to the slain man alone, and God is the Judge. And the 'Alawi vowed to God Almighty that he would not interfere with people in their creeds. And in the letter of their two fathers was that the Summoner
In al-Misbah: al-fayj is a body of men, and it is sometimes applied to a single man, its plural then being fuyuj and afyaj. In al-Sirah: al-fayj is arabicized from the Persian payk.

73.text: al-Hasan b. Zayd had sent to us one of his trusted men with his letter and his seal, giving surety, and had guaranteed to us the return of our properties and the making good of the loss that had befallen us in them; and that we were setting out for the town to obtain what had been promised us (1). The Imam, peace be upon him, said: "Surely God's promise is true." Then on the tenth day there came to us the letter of our two fathers, saying that the Summoner had fulfilled for them all his promises (2), and commanding us to keep close to the Imam of great blessing, the truthful in promise. When the Imam, peace be upon him, heard this, he said: This is the time of my fulfilling what I promised you of the commentary of the Qur'an. Then he said: I have appointed for you each day some portion of it, which you are to write down. So keep close to me and be constant in it, and God Almighty will make abundant your portions of felicity.

I say: in some copies the beginning of the chain runs thus: Muhammad b. 'Ali b. Muhammad b. Ja'far b. al-Daqqaq said: There related to me the two Shaykhs, the two jurists, Abu al-Hasan Muhammad b. Ahmad b. 'Ali b. al-Hasan b. Shadhan and Abu Muhammad Ja'far b. Ahmad b. 'Ali al-Qummi, may God have mercy on them both, who said: There related to us the Shaykh, the jurist, Abu Ja'far Muhammad b. 'Ali b. al-Husayn b. Musa b. Babawayh, may God have mercy on him — to the end of what has passed.

And al-Saduq said in the Kitab Ikmal al-Din: The Shaykh, the jurist, Abu Ja'far Muhammad b. 'Ali b. al-Husayn b. Musa b. Babawayh al-Qummi, the compiler of this book — may God aid him in obeying Him — said: What called me to compose this book of mine was that, when I had fulfilled my desire of visiting 'Ali b. Musa al-Rida, God's blessings be upon him, I returned to Naysabur and stayed there. And I found that most of those of the Shi'a who frequented me had been bewildered by the occultation, and that doubt had entered upon them in the matter of the Qa'im, peace be upon him, and that they had turned from the way of submission to opinions and analogies. So I set about expending my utmost effort (3) in guiding them to the truth and returning them to what is right, by means of the reports that have come down concerning that from the Prophet and the Imams, God's blessings be upon them — until there came to us from Bukhara a shaykh from among the people of excellence, learning and distinction (4) in the town of Qum, whose meeting I had long wished for and whose sight I had longed for, on account of his religion, the soundness of his judgement and the straightness of his way: the Shaykh al-Din Abu Sa'id Muhammad b. al-Hasan b. 'Ali b. Muhammad b. Ahmad b. 'Ali b. al-Salt al-Qummi, may God perpetuate his success.
That is, seeking the speedy discharge of what had been promised us.
That is, my capacity and my power.
Al-nabaha, with fatha on the nun: nobility, acuteness — the opposite of obscurity.

74.text: And my father, may God be pleased with him, used to relate from his grandfather Muhammad b. Ahmad b. 'Ali b. al-Salt, may God sanctify his spirit, and would describe his learning, his excellence, his abstinence and his worship. And Ahmad b. Muhammad b. 'Isa, for all his excellence and eminence, used to relate from Abu Talib 'Abd Allah b. al-Salt al-Qummi (1), may God be pleased with him; and he lived on until Muhammad b. al-Hasan al-Saffar met him and related from him. So when God, exalted be His mention, granted me the good fortune of this shaykh, who is of the people of this lofty house, I thanked God, exalted be His mention, for what He made easy for me of meeting him, and honoured me with of his brotherhood, and bestowed upon me (2) of his affection and his sincerity. Now while he was speaking with me one day, he mentioned to me, concerning a man he had met at Bukhara from among the great philosophers and logicians, words about the Qa'im, peace be upon him, which had bewildered him and made him doubt his affair, on account of the length of his occultation and the cutting off of news of him. So I set out for him sections establishing his existence, and related to him reports concerning his occultation from the Prophet and the Imams, God's blessings be upon them, by which his soul was set at rest, and by which there departed from his heart the doubt, misgiving and confusion that had entered upon him; and he received what he heard of the sound traditions with hearing, obedience, acceptance and submission. And he asked me to compose a book on this subject. So I answered his request, and promised him to gather what he sought when God should make easy the return to my abode and my homeland at Rayy. Then one night, while I was thinking of what I had left behind me of family, children, brethren and blessings, sleep overcame me, and I saw as though I were at Mecca circling the Sacred House, and I was in the seventh circuit at the Black Stone, touching it and kissing it and saying: My trust I have discharged, and my covenant I have kept, that you may bear witness for me to the fulfilment. And I saw our master the Qa'im, the Lord of the Age, God's blessings be upon him, standing at the door of the Ka'ba. So I drew near to him with a preoccupied heart and a divided mind; and he, peace be upon him, knew what was in my soul by reading it in my face. I greeted him, and he returned the greeting, then said to me: Why do you not compose a book on the occultation, so as to be spared what has troubled you? I said to him: O son of the Messenger of God, I have composed things on the occultation. He, God's blessings be upon him, said: Not in that manner do I command you to compose; rather compose now a book on the occultation, and mention in it the occultations of the prophets, peace be upon them.

Al-Najashi, al-Shaykh, al-'Allama and others gave his entry in their books of rijal and stated his trustworthiness plainly. Al-Najashi said, at p. 150: 'Abd Allah b. al-Salt, Abu Talib al-Qummi, client of Banu Taym al-Lat b. Tha'laba, trustworthy, one whose narration is relied upon; he related from al-Rida, peace be upon him; a Kitab al-Tafsir is known to be his. There informed me a number of our companions, from Ahmad b. Muhammad b. Yahya, who said: There related to us 'Abd Allah b. Ja'far, who said: There related to us 'Ali b. 'Abd Allah b. al-Salt, from his father.
Haba such a one, or with such a thing: gave it to him without recompense.

75.text: Then he, God's blessings be upon him, departed; and I awoke in alarm, and turned to supplication and weeping and the pouring out of grief and complaint, until the break of dawn. And when morning came I began the composition of this book, in compliance with the command of the friend of God and His proof, seeking help from God and relying upon Him and asking forgiveness for shortcoming. And my success is only through God; upon Him I rely and to Him I turn.

And Ahmad b. 'Ali al-Tabrisi said in al-Ihtijaj: In most of the reports we set down we do not give the chain — either because there is consensus upon it, or because it accords with what the intellects have indicated, or because of its fame in the biographies and the books among those who differ and those who agree — except what I have set down from Abu Muhammad al-Hasan b. 'Ali al-'Askari, peace be upon them both; for that is not as widely known as the rest, even though it comprises the like of what we have mentioned. For that reason I have given its chain at the first report of it and not elsewhere, since all that I have related from him, peace be upon him, I have related by a single chain, from among the reports which he, peace be upon him, mentioned in his commentary.

Then he said: There related it to me the Sayyid, the learned, the devout, the just, Abu Ja'far Mahdi b. al-'Abid Abu al-Harb al-Husayni al-Mar'ashi, may God be pleased with him. He said: There related to me the Shaykh al-Saduq Abu 'Abd Allah Ja'far b. Muhammad b. Ahmad al-Duristi, may God have mercy on him. He said: There related to me my father Muhammad b. Ahmad. He said: There related to me the Shaykh, the felicitous, Abu Ja'far Muhammad b. 'Ali b. al-Husayn b. Babawayh al-Qummi. He said: There related to me Abu al-Hasan Muhammad b. al-Qasim al-Astarabadi the commentator. He said: There related to me Abu Ya'qub Yusuf b. Muhammad b. Ziyad and Abu al-Hasan 'Ali b. Muhammad b. Sayyar — and the two of them were of the Imami Shi'a — from their fathers, who said: There related to us Abu Muhammad al-Hasan b. 'Ali al-'Askari.

And the Shaykh Ibn Quluwayh, may God have mercy on him, said at the opening of the Kitab Kamil al-Ziyara: And I have gathered it from the Imams, God's blessings be upon them, and have not set down in it a tradition related from other than them, since in what we have related from them of their traditions, God's blessings be upon them, there is sufficiency in place of the traditions of others. And we know that we do not encompass all that has been related from them on this subject, nor on any other; but what has come to us by way of the trustworthy among our companions, may God have mercy on them, I have set down. Nor have I set down in it a tradition related from the isolated among the men, transmitting that (1) from them, who are not known for narration nor renowned for hadith and learning.
In one copy: transmitting that from those mentioned.

76.text: And I found in some of the old copies, at the opening of the Kitab 'Uyun Akhbar al-Rida, peace be upon him: There related to me the Shaykh, the trusted, the father, Abu al-Husayn 'Ali b. Abi Talib b. Muhammad b. Abi Talib al-Tamimi, the resident. He said: There related to me the Sayyid, the peerless, the jurist, the learned, 'Izz al-Din, the honour of the sayyids, Abu Muhammad Sharaf Shah b. Abi al-Futuh Muhammad b. al-Husayn b. Ziyad al-'Alawi al-Husayni al-Aftasi al-Naysaburi — may God perpetuate his elevation — in the months of the year five hundred and seventy-three, at the shrine of our master the Commander of the Faithful 'Ali b. Abi Talib, God's blessings be upon him, during his residence there. He said: There related to me the Shaykh, the jurist, the learned, Abu al-Hasan 'Ali b. 'Abd al-Samad al-Tamimi, may God be pleased with him, in his house at Naysabur in the months of the year five hundred and forty-one. He said: There related to me the Sayyid, the Imam, the ascetic, Abu al-Barakat al-Khuzi, may God be pleased with him. He said: There related to me the Shaykh, the Imam, the learned, the peerless, Abu Ja'far Muhammad b. 'Ali b. al-Husayn b. Musa b. Babawayh al-Qummi, the jurist, the compiler of this book, may God be pleased with him.

And let us mention what we found at the opening of the Kitab Sulaym b. Qays (1), which is this: There informed me the chief, the chaste, Abu al-Tuqa (2) Hibat Allah b. Nama b. 'Ali b. Hamdun, may God be pleased with him, by recitation to him at his house in Hilla of the Two Mosques in Jumada al-Ula of the year five hundred and sixty-five. He said: There related to me the Shaykh, the trusted, the learned, Abu 'Abd Allah al-Husayn b. Ahmad b. Tahhal al-Miqdadi, the resident, by recitation to him at the shrine of our master the Commander of the Faithful, God's blessings be upon him, in the year five hundred and twenty. He said: There related to us the Shaykh al-Mufid Abu 'Ali al-Hasan b. Muhammad al-Tusi, may God be pleased with him, in Rajab of the year four hundred and ninety. And there informed me the Shaykh, the jurist, Abu 'Abd Allah al-Hasan b. Hibat Allah b. Rutba, from the Shaykh al-Mufid Abu 'Ali, from his father, in what I heard being recited to him at the shrine of our master the martyred grandson Abu 'Abd Allah al-Husayn b. 'Ali, God's blessings be upon him, in Muharram of the year five hundred and sixty.

It is the earliest book composed in Islam, in the age of the Successors, after the book of 'Ali b. Abi Rafi'. By that the Shi'a gained precedence in composition in the age of the Successors, just as they had that precedence in the age of the Companions. For at a time when some of the Companions held the compiling and recording of traditions to be unlawful, 'Ali b. Abi Talib, peace be upon him, gathered the Qur'an and composed the Kitab al-Diyat; and he, peace be upon him, had before that, in the age of the Prophet — may God bless him and his family — composed his book of hadith by the dictation of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family. And Salman composed his book on the tradition of the Catholicos, and Abu Dharr his book on what came to pass after the Messenger.

77.text: And there informed me the Shaykh, the reciter, Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad b. al-Kal (1), from the noble, the eminent, Nizam al-Sharaf Abu al-Hasan al-'Uraydi, from Ibn Shahriyar the treasurer, from the Shaykh Abu Ja'far al-Tusi.

And there informed me the Shaykh, the jurist, Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad b. 'Ali b. Shahrashub, by recitation to him at Hilla of the Two Mosques in the months of the year five hundred and sixty-seven, from his grandfather Shahrashub, from the Shaykh, the felicitous, Abu Ja'far Muhammad b. al-Hasan al-Tusi, may God be pleased with him. He said: There related to us Ibn Abi Jayd, from Muhammad b. al-Hasan b. Ahmad b. al-Walid and Muhammad b. Abi al-Qasim, styled Majilawayh, from Muhammad b. 'Ali al-Sayrafi, from Hammad b. 'Isa, from Aban b. Abi 'Ayyash, from Sulaym b. Qays al-Hilali.

The Shaykh Abu Ja'far said: And there informed us Abu 'Abd Allah al-Husayn b. 'Ubayd Allah al-Ghada'iri. He said: There informed us Abu Muhammad Harun b. Musa b. Ahmad al-Tal'ukbari, may God have mercy on him. He said: There informed us 'Ali b. Hammam b. Suhayl. He said: There informed us 'Abd Allah b. Ja'far al-Himyari, from Ya'qub b. Yazid and Muhammad b. al-Husayn b. Abi al-Khattab and Ahmad b. Muhammad b. 'Isa, from Muhammad b. Abi 'Umayr, from 'Umar b. Udhayna, from Aban b. Abi 'Ayyash, from Sulaym b. Qays al-Hilali.

'Umar b. Udhayna said: Ibn Abi 'Ayyash called me and said to me: I saw a dream last night, and I am likely to die soon. I saw you this morning and rejoiced at you. Last night I saw Sulaym b. Qays al-Hilali, and he said to me: Aban, you will die in these days of yours. So fear God concerning my trust and do not squander it, and fulfil for me what you guaranteed of keeping it hidden, and place it only with a man of the Shi'a of 'Ali b. Abi Talib, God's blessings be upon him, who has religion and standing. So when I caught sight of you this morning I rejoiced at seeing you, and remembered my dream of Sulaym b. Qays.

When al-Hajjaj came to Iraq he asked after Sulaym b. Qays, and he fled from him and came upon us at Nawbandajan (2) in hiding, and lodged with us in the house. I never saw a man of greater self-respect, nor more intense in striving, nor longer in hatred of appetite, than he. And I at that time was fourteen years old and had read the Qur'an. I would question him, and he would relate to me from the people of Badr. And I heard from him many traditions from 'Umar b. Abi Salama, the son of

Al-Firuzabadi said: Nawbandajan, with fatha on the nun, the ba' and the undotted dal, is the chief town of the district of Sabur. And he also said: Sabur is a district in Fars whose city is Nawbandajan.

78.text: Umm Salama, the wife of the Prophet, may God bless him and his family; and from Mu'adh b. Jabal, and from Salman al-Farisi, and from 'Ali and Abu Dharr and al-Miqdad and 'Ammar and al-Bara' b. 'Azib. Then he handed them over to me, and did not take an oath from me. It was not long before death came upon him, and he called me and was alone with me and said: Aban, I have been your neighbour and have seen from you only what I love. And with me are books I heard from the trustworthy and wrote with my own hand, in which are traditions I do not like to have made public to people, because people deny them and think them monstrous — yet they are truth, which I took from the people of truth, understanding, veracity and piety: from 'Ali b. Abi Talib, God's blessings be upon him, and Salman al-Farisi and Abu Dharr al-Ghifari and al-Miqdad b. al-Aswad. There is not among them a tradition I heard from one of them but that I asked another about it, until they all agreed upon it; and there are things besides which I heard from others of the people of truth. And when I fell ill I resolved to burn them, but I felt it a sin and held back from it. So if you will give me God's covenant and His compact that you will not inform anyone of them so long as I am alive, and will not relate anything of them after my death except to one you trust as you trust yourself; and that if anything befalls you, you will hand them to one you trust from among the Shi'a of 'Ali b. Abi Talib, God's blessings be upon him, who has religion and standing — then I guaranteed that to him, and he handed them to me and read them all to me. Sulaym did not tarry long before he perished, may God have mercy on him. And I looked into them after him, and held firmly to them, and thought them momentous, and found them hard — because in them is the perdition of the whole community of Muhammad, may God bless him and his family, of the Emigrants and the Helpers and the Successors, save 'Ali b. Abi Talib and the people of his house, God's blessings be upon them, and his Shi'a. And the first I met after my arrival at Basra was al-Hasan b. Abi al-Hasan al-Basri; and he at that time was in hiding from al-Hajjaj, and al-Hasan at that time was of the Shi'a of 'Ali b. Abi Talib, God's blessings be upon him, among those who went to excess in that — regretful and grieved at what he had missed of aiding 'Ali, peace be upon him, and fighting alongside him on the Day of the Camel. So I was alone with him in the eastern part of the house of Abu Khalifa al-Hajjaj b. Abi 'Attab, and laid them before him. He wept, then said: There is nothing in his traditions but truth; I have heard it from the trustworthy among the Shi'a of 'Ali, God's blessings be upon him, and from others.

Aban said: And I made the pilgrimage that year of mine, and entered upon 'Ali b. al-Husayn, peace be upon them both. With him was Abu al-Tufayl 'Amir b. Wathila, the companion of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family, who was among the best of the companions of 'Ali, peace be upon him. And I met with him 'Umar b. Abi Salama, the son of Umm Salama, the wife of the Prophet, may God bless him and his family. So I laid it before him, and I laid all of that before 'Ali b. al-Husayn, God's blessings be upon him, for three days, each day until nightfall; and there would come in the morning

79.text: to him 'Umar and 'Amir. So I read it to him for three days, and he said to me: Sulaym spoke truly, may God have mercy on him; this is all our tradition, we recognize it. And Abu al-Tufayl and 'Umar b. Abi Salama said: There is not in it a tradition but that we have heard it from 'Ali, God's blessings be upon him, and from Salman and from Abu Dharr and al-Miqdad.
'Umar b. Udhayna said: Then Aban handed to me the books of Sulaym b. Qays al-Hilali; and Aban did not tarry after that more than a month before he died.

This is a copy of the book of Sulaym b. Qays al-'Amiri, which he handed to Aban b. Abi 'Ayyash, and which he read to me. And Aban mentioned that he read it to 'Ali b. al-Husayn, peace be upon them both, and he, peace be upon him, said: Sulaym spoke truly; this is our tradition, we recognize it. End of quotation.

I say: the completion of that will come in the Kitab al-Fitan; and we shall set down the remaining prefaces of the books and their chains in the twenty-fifth volume, if God the Exalted wills. And since we have finished what we intended to set down in the introduction to the book, let us mention the index of the books our book comprises and their arrangement; then let us begin setting down the matters in their chapters. There is no power and no strength save in God; upon Him is the reliance, and to Him is the return.
1. The Book of Intellect, Knowledge and Ignorance.
3. The Book of Justice and the Return.
4. The Book of Disputations, Debates and the Comprehensive Sciences.
5. The Book of the Stories of the Prophets, peace be upon them.
6. The Book of the History of our Prophet and his circumstances, may God bless him and his family.
7. The Book of the Imamate, comprising the general circumstances of the Imams, peace be upon them.

8. The Book of the Trials, comprising what came to pass after the Prophet — may God bless him and his family — of the usurpation of the caliphate, and the campaigns of the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him.
9. The Book of the History of the Commander of the Faithful, God's blessings be upon him, his virtues and his circumstances.

80.text: 10. The Book of the History of Fatima, al-Hasan and al-Husayn, God's blessings be upon them, their virtues and their miracles.
11. The Book of the History of 'Ali b. al-Husayn, Muhammad b. 'Ali al-Baqir, Ja'far b. Muhammad al-Sadiq and Musa b. Ja'far al-Kazim, God's blessings be upon them, their virtues and their miracles.

12. The Book of the History of 'Ali b. Musa al-Rida, Muhammad b. 'Ali al-Jawad, 'Ali b. Muhammad al-Hadi and al-Hasan b. 'Ali al-'Askari, their circumstances and their miracles, God's blessings be upon them.
13. The Book of the Occultation and the circumstances of the Proof, the Qa'im, God's blessings be upon him.

14. The Book of the Heaven and the World, comprising the circumstances of the Throne, the Footstool, the celestial spheres, the elements, the generated beings, the angels, the jinn, mankind, the beasts, the birds and the rest of the animals; and in it are the chapters on hunting and slaughter, and the chapters on medicine.
15. The Book of Faith, Unbelief and Nobility of Character.
16. The Book of Manners, Practices, Commands, Prohibitions, Grave Sins and Acts of Disobedience; and in it are the chapters on the prescribed penalties.
17. The Book of the Garden, comprising the admonitions, the maxims and the sermons.
18. The Book of Purity and Prayer.
19. The Book of the Qur'an and Supplication.
20. The Book of Alms and Fasting; and in it are the works of the year.
23. The Book of Contracts and Unilateral Dispositions.
25. The Book of Licences — and it is the last of the books, comprising our chains and our routes to all the books, and the licences of the eminent scholars, God's pleasure be upon them all.

81.text: The Book of Intellect, Knowledge and Ignorance
Chapter 1: The merit of the intellect and the censure of ignorance

al-Baqara: "signs for a people who use their intellect"; and He, exalted, said: "thus does God make clear to you His signs, that perhaps you may understand"; and He, exalted, said: "yet none takes heed save those possessed of understanding."

Al 'Imran: "yet none takes heed save those possessed of understanding"; and He, exalted, said: "We have made clear to you the signs, if you would use your intellect"; and He said: "truly in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, there are signs for those possessed of understanding."

al-Ma'ida: "that is because they are a people who do not use their intellect"; and He, exalted, said: "so fear God, O you possessed of understanding"; and He said: "and most of them do not use their intellect."
al-An'am: "but most of them are ignorant"; and He said: "and surely the abode of the hereafter is better for those who are godfearing — will you not then use your intellect?"
al-Anfal: "truly the worst of creatures in God's sight are the deaf and dumb who do not use their intellect."
Yunus: "can you then make the deaf hear, though they do not use their intellect?"; and He, exalted, said: "and He lays defilement upon those who do not use their intellect."
Hud: "but I see you are a people who are ignorant."
Yusuf: "truly We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, that perhaps you may understand."
al-Ra'd: "only those possessed of understanding take heed."
Ibrahim: "and that those possessed of understanding may take heed."
Ta Ha: "truly in that are signs for those possessed of reason."
al-Nur: "thus does God make clear to you the signs, that perhaps you may understand."
al-Zumar: "truly in that is a reminder for those possessed of understanding."

82.text: al-Mu'min: "a guidance and a reminder for those possessed of understanding"; and He, exalted, said: "and that perhaps you may understand."
al-Jathiya: "signs for a people who use their intellect."
al-Hujurat: "most of them do not use their intellect."
al-Hadid: "We have made clear to you the signs, that perhaps you may understand."
al-Hashr: "that is because they are a people who do not use their intellect."

«1»- Ma'ani al-Akhbar; al-Amali of al-Saduq: al-Hafiz, from Ahmad b. 'Abd Allah al-Thaqafi, from 'Isa b. Muhammad al-Katib, from al-Mada'ini, from Ghiyath b. Ibrahim, from al-Sadiq Ja'far b. Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather, peace be upon him, who said: 'Ali b. Abi Talib, peace be upon them both, said: The intellects of women lie in their beauty, and the beauty of men lies in their intellects. (1)

Exposition: al-jamal (beauty) is excellence in form and in character. As for his saying, peace be upon him, "the intellects of women lie in their beauty" — the meaning may be that one ought not to look to their intellect, given its rarity, but rather be content with their beauty; or the meaning may be that their intellect is for the most part bound up with their beauty. The first is the more evident.

«2»- al-Amali of al-Saduq: al-'Attar, from his father, from Sahl, from Muhammad b. 'Isa, from al-Bazanti, from Jamil, from al-Sadiq Ja'far b. Muhammad, peace be upon them both, who said: The Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, used to say: The root of a man is his understanding, his intellect is his religion, and his manliness is where he places himself. The days are turns of fortune, and people are equal in their descent from Adam.

Exposition: al-lubb, with a damma on the lam, is the pure essence of anything, and also the intellect; the second is what is meant here. That is, the precedence of individual men in the nobility of their origin rests upon their intellects, not upon their lineages or their ancestral merits. Then he, peace be upon him, explained that the intellect which is the source of nobility appears only through choosing the true religion from among the religions, and through perfecting one's religion with the things that perfect faith. And al-muruwwa, with hamza and with a damma on the mim and the ra', is humanity (2), derived from al-mar' (man); it is sometimes lightened by substitution and assimilation. What is apparently meant is that a man's humanity, and his completeness or deficiency therein,

It may be that his intent, peace be upon him, was to urge men and encourage them toward what perfects their intellects, and to press them to abandon the adorning of their beauty and what pertains to their outward appearance. It is as when you say to a man: How much do you care for improving your appearance, the cleanliness of your face, the curling of your hair?! Leave that to women — a man's beauty lies only in perfecting his intellect and purifying his soul. On this reading, what is meant by "beauty" is excellence of outward form and of character.

He erred here, God have mercy on him, for derivations of this kind — insaniyya (humanity), muruwwa (manliness), futuwwa (chivalry) and the like — serve to convey the appearance of the effects of the root from which they derive. So the meaning of muruwwa is the appearance in a person of the qualities of the man (al-mar') as against the woman (al-mar'a): loftiness of outlook, overlooking petty faults rather than disputing them, fidelity, and the like.

83.text: …the lofty ranks and the base stations. How wide is the gap between one who is content for himself with nothing short of the full rank of knowledge, obedience, nearness and union, and one who is content to be a laughing-stock for base men for the sake of a meal or a morsel, and sees for himself no honour or standing beyond that.
It may also be that what is meant is marrying among one's equals, as
al-Sadiq, peace be upon him, said to Dawud al-Karkhi when he wished to marry: Look where you are placing yourself.
But the general sense is the more evident.

Al-duwal — the dal taking any of the three vowels — is the plural of dawla, with damma or with fatha, both meaning the turning of time and the passing of wealth or of might from one person to another; with damma it also means victory in war. The meaning is that dominion over this world, its possession and its might belong one day to one people and another day to others. And "people are, with respect to Adam, shara'" — with the ra' unvowelled, though it is sometimes vowelled — that is, equal in lineage, all of them children of Adam. So these shifting, perishing things do not become the measure of nobility; rather nobility lies in the real and enduring things that last in both abodes. The last two clauses reinforce the first two.

«3»- al-Amali of al-Saduq: Ibn Idris, from his father, from Ibn Hashim, from Ibn Marrar, from Yunus, from Ibn Sinan (1), from al-Sadiq Ja'far b. Muhammad, peace be upon them both, who said: Five things — whoever lacks them has little in him from which benefit is drawn. It was said: And what are they, O son of the Messenger of God? He said: Religion, intellect, modesty, good character and good breeding. And five things — whoever lacks them, life is not pleasant for him: health, security, sufficiency, contentment, and a congenial companion.

«4»- al-Khisal: My father, from Sa'd, from Ibn Yazid, from Isma'il b. Qutayba al-Basri, from Abu Khalid al-'Ajami, from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, who said: Five things — whoever lacks them has little in him from which benefit is drawn: religion, intellect, good breeding, freedom and good character.
al-Mahasin: Ibn Yazid, the like of it, except that it has "generosity" in place of "freedom".

Exposition: Good breeding (husn al-adab) is the conducting of one's affairs by the rule of the Sacred Law and of the intellect, in the service of the Truth and in dealing with created beings. And sufficiency (al-ghina) is to have no need of created beings — that is, sufficiency of soul, for that is the perfection, not

With a kasra on the unpointed sin and a fatha on the nun. It appears he is 'Abd Allah b. Sinan, who — as in the Rijal of al-Najashi — is Ibn Tarif, a client of the Banu Hashim, though it is also said a client of the Banu Abi Talib. He was treasurer to al-Mansur, al-Mahdi, al-Hadi and al-Rashid; a Kufan, trustworthy, one of our companions, of high standing, against whom nothing at all is impugned. He narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him. It has been said that he narrated from Abu al-Hasan Musa, peace be upon him, but that is not established, since Muhammad b. Sinan did not narrate from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him.

84.text: …sufficiency through wealth. As for "freedom", it may carry its apparent meaning, for it is a perfection in this world and its opposite is generally an obstacle to attaining the perfections of the hereafter; and it may be that what is meant by it is emancipation from bondage to the appetites of the soul and release from captivity to satanic whisperings. And God knows best.
«5»- al-Amali of al-Saduq: There is no beauty more adorning than the intellect.
He narrated it within a long sermon from the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him; its full text will come in the chapter on his sermons, peace be upon him.

«6»- al-Amali of al-Saduq: Ibn Musa, from Muhammad b. Ya'qub, from 'Ali b. Muhammad b. 'Abd Allah, from Ibrahim b. Ishaq al-Ahmar, from Muhammad b. Sulayman, from his father, who said: I said to Abu 'Abd Allah al-Sadiq, peace be upon him: So-and-so, in his worship, his religion and his merit, is such and such. He said: How is his intellect? I said: I do not know. He said: Reward is according to the measure of the intellect. There was a man of the Children of Israel who used to worship God, mighty and exalted, on an island among the islands of the sea — green, verdant, thick with trees, with pure water. An angel among the angels passed by him and said: My Lord, show me the reward of this servant of Yours. So God, mighty and exalted, showed it to him, and the angel thought it little. Then God, mighty and exalted, revealed to him: Keep his company. So the angel came to him in the form of a man, and he said to him: Who are you? He said: I am a worshipping man; word of your place and your worship here reached us, so I have come to worship alongside you. He stayed with him that day, and when morning came the angel said to him: Your place here is truly a pleasant one. He said: Would that our Lord had a beast! If our Lord had a donkey we would pasture it in this spot, for this grass is going to waste. The angel said to him: But your Lord has no donkey. He said: Had He a donkey, grass such as this would not be going to waste. Then God, mighty and exalted, revealed to the angel: I reward him only according to the measure of his intellect. (1)

It may be said that what is meant by the reward is what is prepared for the weak and the simple-minded; or it may be said that reward follows upon the spirit of obedience and upon the servant's being compliant and obedient to his Master's command, just as punishment follows upon disobedience and upon his being in a posture of insolence and obstinacy. Since this worshipper was a believer, compliant toward God, exalted, reward follows upon his faith and his compliance even though he fell short in grasping some of God's attributes. And so you see that out of his love and compliance toward the Master he wishes the benefit to return to Him, glory be to Him, as is suggested by his words "Would that our Lord had a beast" and "If our Lord had a donkey we would pasture it" — all of this on the assumption that the report indicates his believing in corporeality. And it may be said that the soundness of a person's choices discloses the completeness of his intellect, and the absence of such soundness discloses its absence; so choosing the impossible when the possible could be chosen, or preferring the baser thing — pasturing his donkey — over the nobler, which is intimate discourse with God and worship of Him, discloses the deficiency of his intellect. On this reading the worshipper was not one who held God, glory be to Him, to be corporeal, as the phrase "if I were entrusted with it" suggests; but since his intellect was deficient, the full reward did not befit him.

85.text: «7»- And al-Sadiq, peace be upon him, said: The Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — never spoke to the servants with the full depth of his intellect. He said: And the Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: We, the company of prophets, have been commanded to speak to people according to the measure of their intellects.

Elucidation: It appears that his words "And al-Sadiq, peace be upon him, said", to the end of the report, are a chainless report, as appears from al-Kafi. His words "of his worship" are an explanation of his words "such and such"; and "such and such" is the predicate of his words "so-and-so". It is possible that it relates to something understood — that is, "and I mentioned of his worship" — and possible that it relates to what was expressed by "such and such", as in his words "excellent, complete". So the word min has the sense of fi, or is causal. Al-nadara is beauty; and al-tahara here is in its lexical sense, that is, purity and delicacy.

And in some copies of al-Kafi it is with the dotted za', that is, it was flowing over the face of the earth. Al-nazaha is remoteness from what entails ugliness and corruption. More evident is li-nazzih, as in al-Kafi; and perhaps it is by way of construing it as the plot, the courtyard and the like.

And in the report there is a difficulty, in that its apparent sense is that the worshipper held to corporeality, and this is incompatible with his deserving reward at all; whereas the apparent sense of the report is that, with this corrupt belief, he deserved reward on account of the smallness of his intellect and his simplicity. It is possible that the lam in his words "that our Lord had a beast" is for possession and not for benefit, and that what he meant was to wish that there might be in this place a beast from among the beasts of the Lord, so that the grass should not go to waste. In that case the deficiency of his intellect would be by reason of his not knowing the benefits of the things God the Exalted has made — that they are not confined to being eaten by beasts. But the angel's answer resists this, unless it be to ward off what his words might suggest, or unless it be a rhetorical question of denial — that is, God the Exalted has created many beasts that profit from the grass of the earth, and this is one of the benefits of creating grass, and they have been ordered according to the measure of the good. It is not required that there be an ass in this place; rather your existence and your profiting suffice.

And it is possible that the lam is for particular relation, not for mere ownership — such that this beast should have a particular relation to the Lord, exalted be He, as His House has a particular relation to Him, exalted be He, notwithstanding His having no need of it. And the angel's answer would then be that there is no benefit in such a creation, that God the Exalted should create an ass and ascribe it to His sacred presence, as is the case with the House — for in that there are many wise purposes.
And on all these suppositions one must either undertake a thorough forced construction of the words, or else accept the falsity of some

86.text: of the principles established in theology. And God knows.

«8»- l, al-Khisal; li, the Amali of al-Saduq: Ibn al-Barqi, from his father, from his grandfather, from 'Amr b. 'Uthman, from Abu Jamila (1), from Ibn Tarif (2), from Ibn Nubata (3), from 'Ali b. Abi Talib, peace be upon them both, who said: Gabriel descended upon Adam, peace be upon him, and said: Adam, I have been commanded to give you a choice of one of three; so choose one and leave two. Adam said to him: And what are the three, Gabriel? He said: Intellect, modesty and religion (4). Adam said: Then I have chosen the intellect. So Gabriel said to modesty and religion: Depart. And he called him; and they said to him: Gabriel, we have been commanded (5) to be with the intellect wherever it is. He said: Then to your business. And he ascended.

sn, al-Mahasin: 'Amr b. 'Uthman, the like of it. Elucidation: al-sha'n, with the hamza, is the affair and the state — that is, keep to your business, or your business is with you. Perhaps the purpose was to alert Adam, peace be upon him, and his children to the greatness of the blessing of the intellect. It has been said that the discourse rests upon representational metaphor. And it is possible that Gabriel, peace be upon him, brought three forms, in place of each of the qualities a form suited to it; for each of the accidents and the intelligibles has a form suited to it among bodies and sensibles, and by these they are represented in dreams, and indeed in the hereafter. And God knows.
«9»- l, al-Khisal: Ibn al-Walid, from al-Saffar, from Muhammad b. 'Isa, from 'Uthman b. 'Isa, from
He is al-Mufaddal b. Salih al-Asadi al-Nakhkhas, with damma on the nun and a doubled dotted kha'. He was charged with extremism, weakness, lying and the fabrication of hadith.

With undotted ta' and ra', on the pattern of amir. He is Sa'd b. Tarif al-Hanzali al-Iskaf, client of Banu Tamim, of Kufa. Al-Shaykh counted him among the companions of al-Sajjad, al-Baqir and al-Sadiq, peace be upon them, and said: He related from al-Asbagh b. Nubata, and he is sound in hadith.

With damma on the nun. He is al-Asbagh, with fatha on the hamza, son of Nubata al-Tamimi al-Hanzali al-Mujashi'i, of Kufa. Al-Najashi said: He was of the intimates of the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, and lived on after him. From him are related the covenant of al-Ashtar and his testament to his son Muhammad.

What is meant by al-'aql here is a divine subtlety by which man perceives the reality of things and distinguishes between good and evil, truth and falsehood, and by which he knows what pertains to the origin and the return. It has degrees according to strength and weakness. And al-haya' is an innate disposition preventing the commission of base acts and shortcoming in the rights of the Truth and of creation. And al-din is that by which people's welfare and advancement in this life and the next are secured, whether by natural dispositions or by positive laws.
Perhaps what is meant by the command is the creative, not the legislative — that is, the intellect's entailing modesty and religion, and their following upon it.

87.text: Ibn Muskan (1), from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, who said: Nothing less than five has been apportioned among the servants: certainty, contentment, patience, gratitude — and that by which all this is made complete, the intellect.

sn, al-Mahasin: 'Uthman b. 'Isa, the like of it. Elucidation: that is, these qualities are found among people less than the rest of the qualities; and whoever has intellect, all of them are in him in their completeness. So it indicates the rarity of the intellect as well.
«10»- l, al-Khisal, in the Four Hundred: Whoever's intellect is complete, his deed is good.

«11»- n, 'Uyun Akhbar al-Rida, peace be upon him: al-Daqqaq, from al-Asadi, from Ahmad b. Muhammad b. Salih al-Razi, from Hamdan al-Diwani, who said: al-Rida, peace be upon him, said: Every man's friend is his intellect, and his enemy is his ignorance (2).

With damma on the mim and sukun on the undotted sin; it is the name of the father of 'Abd Allah. Al-Najashi said, p. 148: 'Abd Allah b. Muskan, Abu Muhammad, client of 'Anaza, trustworthy, a man of note; he related from Abu al-Hasan Musa, peace be upon him. It is said that he related from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, but that is not established. He has books, among them a book on the Imamate and a book on the lawful and the unlawful, most of it from Muhammad b. 'Ali b. Abi Shu'ba al-Halabi. And he mentioned his routes to him, then said after it: He died in the days of Abu al-Hasan, before the incident. Al-Kashshi counted him, at p. 239, among those upon whose soundness the party has agreed — accepting what is soundly transmitted from them, holding them truthful in what they say, and acknowledging their jurisprudence — from among the companions of Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him. And he said at p. 243: He heard from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, only the tradition "Whoever reaches al-Mash'ar has reached the Hajj" — until he said: And Abu al-Nadr Muhammad b. Mas'ud held that Ibn Muskan would not enter upon Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, out of apprehension that he would not render him the full due of his reverence; so he would hear from his companions and refrain from entering upon him, out of reverence and magnification for him, peace be upon him — end of quotation. I say: there are found for him many narrations in the chapters of jurisprudence and elsewhere from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, so much so that it is transmitted from al-Majlisi the First, may God have mercy on him, that they amount to nearly thirty traditions in the Four Books and elsewhere. So the soundness of the statement of al-Najashi and al-Kashshi would require that those traditions be chainless, which is very far-fetched. It is possible to construe their statement as meaning that he did not relate from him, peace be upon him, face to face — so there is no objection to his questioning him, peace be upon him, by correspondence, as al-Kashshi hints in his Rijal. He said: And Yunus held that Ibn Muskan sent questions to Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, asking him about them, and he answered him upon them. Among these is what went out to him with Ibrahim b. Maymun: he wrote to him asking about a eunuch who misrepresented himself to a woman. He said: They are to be separated, and his back is to be beaten.

Because the part of everyone is to bring his friend to what holds his felicity and his benefit, and to repel harms and evils from him; and the part of the enemy is the reverse. And these attributes are stronger and more intense in the intellect and in ignorance — for by the intellect man attains to good things, knows wherein lie felicity and wretchedness, travels the path of guidance and right direction, and distinguishes between truth and falsehood; and by it the Merciful is worshipped and the gardens are earned. And by ignorance he travels the path of error and ignorance, and falls into the abyss of evil and misguidance; and by it Satan is worshipped and the wrath of the Merciful is earned. So the application of "friend" to the intellect is the more fitting, just as the application of "enemy" to ignorance is the more proper.

88.text: And he also related it from his father, and Ibn al-Walid from Sa'd, and al-Himyari from Ibn Hashim, from al-Hasan b. al-Jahm, from al-Rida, peace be upon him. — 'a, 'Ilal al-Shara'i': my father, from Sa'd, from Ibn 'Isa, from Ibn Faddal, from al-Hasan b. al-Jahm, from him, peace be upon him, the like of it. — sn, al-Mahasin: Ibn Faddal, the like of it. — Kanz al-Karajaki, from the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, the like of it.

«12»- ma, the Amali of al-Shaykh al-Tusi: al-Mufid, may God have mercy on him, from Abu Hafs 'Umar b. Muhammad, from Ibn Mahrawayh, from Dawud b. Sulayman, who said: I heard al-Rida, peace be upon him, saying: God has not deposited an intellect with a servant but that He delivered him by it one day.
nhj, the Nahj al-Balagha, the like of it.

«13»- ma, the Amali of al-Shaykh al-Tusi: al-Mufid, from al-Husayn b. Muhammad al-Tammar, from Muhammad b. Qasim al-Anbari, from Ahmad b. 'Ubayd, from 'Abd al-Rahim b. Qays al-Hilali, from al-'Umari, from Abu Hamza al-Sa'di, from his father, who said: The Commander of the Faithful 'Ali b. Abi Talib, peace be upon them both, made his testament to al-Hasan b. 'Ali, peace be upon them both, and said among what he enjoined upon him: My son, there is no poverty more severe than ignorance, and no privation more severe than the privation of intellect; and no solitude and no desolation more desolate than self-admiration; and no standing like goodness of character; and no scrupulousness like restraint from what God has forbidden; and no worship like reflection upon the making of God, Almighty and Glorious. My son, the intellect is a man's close friend, forbearance his vizier, gentleness his father, and patience among the best of his troops. My son, the man of intellect must needs look into his own affair; so let him guard his tongue and know the people of his age. My son, among trials is destitution, and more severe than that is sickness of the body, and more severe than that is sickness of the heart. And among blessings is amplitude of wealth, and better than that is soundness of the body, and better than that is the God-fearing of hearts. My son, the believer has three hours: an hour in which he converses secretly with his Lord; an hour in which he calls himself to account; and an hour in which he is alone with himself and its pleasure in what is lawful and praiseworthy. And the believer must needs set out for three things: the mending of a livelihood (1), or a step towards the hereafter, or a pleasure in what is not forbidden.
Elucidation: al-'udm, with damma, is poverty and the loss of a thing. And al-'ujb is a man's being pleased with himself for his virtues
Ramma an affair: he set it right.

89.text: and his deeds; and it entails raising oneself above people and overbearing them, so that it becomes a cause of people's estrangement from him, and entails abandoning the correction of his faults and the making good of what he has missed. So the sources of God's mercy, His kindness and His guidance are cut off from him, and he is left apart from his Lord and from creation — so there is no desolation more desolate than it. And his words, peace be upon him, "and no scrupulousness", are by comparison with the scrupulousness of one who abstains from things disapproved but does not abstain from things forbidden. Al-shukhus is going from town to town and travelling in the land; and it is possible that what is meant here includes going out from the house. Al-khutwa, with damma and with kasra, is standing, nearness and rank — that is, he sets out to acquire what brings about standing and rank in the hereafter.

«14»- ma, the Amali of al-Shaykh al-Tusi: al-Mufid, from Ibn Quluwayh, from al-Kulayni, from 'Ali b. Ibrahim, from al-Yaqtini, from Hannan b. Sadir, from his father, from al-Baqir, peace be upon him, in the report of Salman and 'Umar, that he said: The Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: Company of Quraysh, a man's standing is his religion, his manliness his character, and his root his intellect.

«15»- ma, the Amali of al-Shaykh al-Tusi: al-Mufid, from Isma'il b. Muhammad al-Katib, from 'Abd al-Samad b. 'Ali, from Muhammad b. Harun b. 'Isa, from Abu Talha al-Khuza'i, from 'Umar b. 'Abbad, from Abu Furat, who said: I read in a book of Wahb b. Munabbih, and there was written at the head of the book: This is what the sages have set down in their books. Striving in the worship of God is the most profitable trade; and there is no wealth more beneficial than intellect; and no poverty more severe than ignorance; and a discipline you acquire is better than an inheritance; and goodness of character is the best companion; and success is the best leader; and there is no support more reliable than consultation; and no desolation more desolate than self-admiration. And let not the man of pride covet fair praise of himself.

Elucidation: al-'a'ida is benefit; and it is said "this is a'wad", that is, more beneficial. And "no support" means no helper and no strengthener — for a man's strength is by the strength of his back.

«16»- 'a, 'Ilal al-Shara'i': Ibn al-Mutawakkil, from al-Sa'dabadi, from al-Barqi, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from one he named, from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, who said: God, Almighty and Glorious, has created nothing more hateful to Him than the fool; for He has stripped him of the most beloved of things to Him, and that is his intellect.

Elucidation: His hatred, exalted be He, is an expression of His knowledge of the baseness of his rank and his lack of capacity for perfection and for what follows upon it; or of His not granting him success in what would require the elevation of his standing, on account of his lack of capacity for that. So it is not incompatible with

90.text: his having no choice in that. Or His hatred, exalted be He, may be for what he chooses by his evil choice of the base among his deeds, while being free to leave it. And God knows (1).

«17»- 'a, 'Ilal al-Shara'i': Ibn al-Walid, from al-Saffar, from Ahmad b. Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from some of his companions, from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, who said: The pillar of man is the intellect; and of the intellect are acuteness, understanding, retention and knowledge. So when the support of his intellect is from the light, he is knowing, retentive, pure, acute, understanding. And by the intellect he is made complete; and it is his guide, his beholder and the key of his affair.

Elucidation: al-di'ama, with kasra, is the pillar of the house. Al-fitna is swiftness in grasping matters aright. And light, since it is a cause of the appearance of sensible things, is applied to everything that becomes a cause of the appearance of things to the sense or to the intellect. So it is applied to knowledge, and to the spirits of the Imams, peace be upon them, and to the mercy of God, glory be to Him, and to what He casts into the hearts of the knowers of clarity and lustre, by which the realities of wisdom and the subtleties of matters are made manifest to them; and to the Lord, blessed and exalted, because He is the Light of lights, and from Him all things appear in outward existence and in the disclosure of knowledge. And here al-jamr is possible. And his words "pure" — in the copies we have seen it is with the za', so it is in the sense of purity from ignorance and from base qualities; and in al-Kafi in its place is "mindful".

«18»- b, Qurb al-Isnad: Harun, from Ibn Sadaqa, from Ja'far b. Muhammad, peace be upon them both, who said: God, blessed and exalted, hates the ignorant old man, the oppressive rich man, and the proud poor man.

Elucidation: The singling out of the ignorant as an old man is because ignorance from him is more repugnant, since a long time has passed in which he might have acquired knowledge. And the singling out of the oppressive as rich is because oppression from him is more outrageous, since he has no need. And the singling out of the proud — that is, the arrogant — as poor is because it is more disgraceful from him; for the rich man, when he is arrogant, has some excuse in that, on account of the boasting, self-admiration and insolence that attach to wealth.

What he intends, may God have mercy on him, is to remove the incompatibility that appears between hatred and the fact that the fool's folly is not traceable to his own choice. And it is not hidden that the incompatibility is not removed by the two aspects he mentioned, may God have mercy on him; for knowledge of the baseness of a rank is not called hatred, and likewise the withholding of success on account of lack of capacity; and what he chooses of the base on account of his folly comes at last to what is not by choice. So the difficulty stands as it was. The truth is that His hatred — as appears from his reasoning, peace be upon him — is in the sense of withholding him from that with which it is man's part to be clothed, namely the intellect, which is the most beloved of things to God, on account of a deficiency in his constitution. So it is a creative hatred, in the sense of distancing from the advantages of the constitution — not a legislative hatred, in the sense of distancing him from forgiveness and the Garden. And what is incompatible with the absence of choice is hatred in the second sense, not the first. T.

91.text: «19»- thw, Thawab al-A'mal: my father, from Ahmad b. Idris, from al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad b. Hassan, from Abu Muhammad al-Razi, from al-Husayn b. Yazid, from Ibrahim b. Bakr b. Abi Sammak, from al-Fadl (1) b. 'Uthman, who said: I heard Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, saying: Whoever is possessed of intellect, his end is sealed with the Garden, if God wills.

«20»- thw, Thawab al-A'mal, by this chain, from Abu Muhammad, from Ibn 'Amira, from Ishaq b. 'Ammar, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, said: Whoever is possessed of intellect has religion; and whoever has religion enters the Garden.

«21»- sn, al-Mahasin: my father, from Muhammad b. Sinan, from a man of Hamdan, from 'Ubayd Allah b. al-Walid al-Wassafi, from Abu Ja'far, peace be upon him, who said: Musa b. 'Imran, peace be upon them both, used to see a man of the Children of Israel whose prostration was long and whose silence was long, so that he would scarcely go to any place but that the man was with him. Now one day, while he was about some of his needs, he passed by a grassy land, verdant and swaying. He said: The man sighed. Musa said to him: At what have you sighed? He said: I wished that my Lord had an ass, that I might pasture it here. He said: And Musa, peace be upon him, cast down his gaze upon the ground a long while, in distress at what he had heard from him. He said: Then the revelation came down upon him, and He said to him: What is it you have thought so grave in the speech of My servant? I take My servants to account according to the measure of what I have given them of intellect.

Elucidation: In al-Qamus, al-zahw is the fair aspect, and fresh growth, and the blossom of a plant, its bloom and its radiance. And al-ihtizaz is movement, briskness and gladness. It appears that the two are with the ta', being adjectives qualifying the land, or circumstantial expressions of it, to indicate the freshness of its herbage, its tenderness and its growth. And if they are with the two ya's, as in most of the copies, it is possible that they are circumstantial expressions of the subject of "passed by", namely the worshipper, in relation to Musa, peace be upon him. Al-zahw also comes in the sense of boasting — that is, he was boasting and being brisk, by way of showing his thanks to Him, exalted be He, for what He had prepared for him of that.

«22»- sn, al-Mahasin: some of our companions, raising it, said: The Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: God has apportioned to the servants nothing more excellent than the intellect. The sleep of the man of intellect is more excellent than the vigil of the ignorant; the breaking of fast of the man of intellect is more excellent than the fasting of the ignorant; and the staying at home of the man of intellect is more excellent than the setting out of the ignorant. And God has not sent a messenger nor a prophet until

92.text: He had made the intellect complete in him, and his intellect was more excellent than the intellects of all his community. And what the prophet keeps within himself is more excellent than the striving of those who strive. And the man of intellect has not performed the obligations of God until he understood from Him. And all the worshippers have not attained, in the excellence of their worship, what the man of intellect has attained. The people of intellect are the possessors of understanding, of whom God, Almighty and Glorious, said: "Only the possessors of understanding take heed."

Clarification: "than the setting out of the ignorant" — that is, his going out from his town and his travelling to the lands in quest of His good pleasure, exalted be He, such as jihad, the pilgrimage and the like. "And what the prophet keeps within himself" — that is, of sound intentions, complete reflections and certain beliefs. "And the man of intellect has not performed the obligations of God until he understood from Him" — that is, he does not perform an obligation until he understands from God and knows that God desired that of him, and knows the proprieties of its performance. It is possible that what is meant is more general than that — that is, he understands and knows what it is incumbent upon him to know. So min is inceptive on both suppositions; and it is possible, though remotely, that it is partitive — that is, he understood of His attributes, His greatness and His majesty what befits his understanding and suits his capacity and preparedness. And in most copies it is "and the intellect has not performed", which comes back to what we have mentioned, since the man of intellect performs by the intellect. And in al-Kafi it is "and the servant has not performed the obligations of God until he understood from Him" — that is, it is not possible for the servant to perform the obligations as they ought to be except by understanding and knowing from a quarter taken from God by revelation, or by God's inspiring him with the knowledge of it, or by God's giving him a bestowed intellect by which he travels the path of deliverance.

«23»- sn, al-Mahasin: some of our companions, raising it, said: No account is taken, among the people of this religion, of one who has no intellect. He said: I said: May I be made your ransom, we come to a people in whom we see no harm, of those who profess this affair, but they do not have those intellects. He said: These are not among those whom God addressed in His words "O possessors of understanding". God created the intellect and said to it: Come forward — and it came forward. Then He said to it: Go back — and it went back. Then He said: By My might and My majesty, I have not created anything fairer than you, nor more beloved to Me than you. By you I take, and by you I give.

Elucidation: "no account is taken" — that is, no regard is had and no heed is paid to the case of one who has no intellect among the people of this religion. So the questioner said: With us are a people who have entered into this religion but are not complete in intellect; how then do they stand? And he, peace be upon him, answered that they, though deprived of the virtues of the people of intellect, yet have their obligations lighter and easier — and most of the addresses concerning burdensome obligations are to the possessors of understanding.

93.text: «24»- sn, al-Mahasin: al-Nawfali and Jahm b. Hakim al-Mada'ini, from al-Sakuni, from Abu 'Abd Allah, from his forefathers, peace be upon them, who said: The Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: When there reaches you concerning a man the goodness of his state, look into the goodness of his intellect; for he is recompensed only according to his intellect.
I say: in al-Kafi it is husn hal, without the pronoun.

«25»- ms, Misbah al-Shari'a: al-Sadiq, peace be upon him, said: Ignorance is a form compounded in the children of Adam. Its approach is darkness and its withdrawal is light; and the servant turns about with it (1) as the shadow turns about with the sun. Do you not see that a man — at one time you find him ignorant of the qualities of his own soul, praising them, recognizing their fault in another and detesting it; and at another time you find him knowing his own dispositions, detesting them, praising them in another? So he turns about between preservation and abandonment: if preservation meets him he hits the mark, and if abandonment meets him he errs. The key of ignorance is contentment with it and belief in it; and the key of knowledge is exchange, together with the attainment of the concurrence of divine success. The least of the description of the ignorant is his claim to knowledge without deserving it; the middle of it is his ignorance of ignorance; and the utmost of it is his denial of knowledge. And there is nothing whose affirmation is in reality its own negation except ignorance, the world, and greed. So the whole of them is as one, and one of them is as the whole.

Elucidation: "as the shadow turns about with the sun" — that is, just as the rays of the sun may overcome the shadow and light up its place, and may at times be the reverse; so likewise knowledge and intellect may prevail over the soul, so that the faults of his own soul appear to him and he construes away, by his intellect, the faults of another as far as he is able; and ignorance may prevail, so that he sees the good qualities of another as faults and the faults of his own soul as good qualities. And the key of ignorance is contentment with ignorance and belief in it, and in its being a perfection not to be parted from; and the key of knowledge is seeking to acquire knowledge in exchange for ignorance, and perfection in exchange for deficiency. And one ought to know that his striving, without the assistance of divine success, does not profit; so let him seek recourse to His presence, exalted be He, that He may grant him success. His words, peace be upon him, "its affirmation", that is, the knowing of it. Al-Firuzabadi said: athbatahu — he knew it with true knowledge. And it is evident that the knowledge of those matters as they are entails the abandoning and the negating of them; or the meaning is that everyone who acknowledges the subsistence of those things inevitably negates them of himself. So what is meant by "the world" is the love of it, and

In one copy: with the two of them. And his words, peace be upon him, "Ignorance is a form compounded" and so on — because man's nature, in the root of its original constitution, is empty of actual perfections and of established knowledge; so ignorance was, as it were, kneaded into its clay and compounded with its nature. Yet in the root of his constitution he has the power to acquire perfections through knowledge, illumination and the divine sciences.

94.text: his words, peace be upon him, "the whole is as one" — perhaps its meaning is that these qualities are like a single quality, on account of the likeness of their origins, the arising of some of them from others, and the strengthening of some of them by others, as is not hidden.

There is no wealth like the intellect, no poverty like ignorance, no inheritance like discipline, no wealth more beneficial than the intellect, and no intellect like good management.

«28»- dh, Rawdat al-Wa'izin: It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The foundation of religion is built upon the intellect, and the obligations were imposed upon the intellect. Our Lord is known by the intellect, and recourse is had to Him by the intellect. And the man of intellect is nearer to his Lord than all those who strive without intellect. An atom's weight of the piety of the man of intellect is more excellent than a thousand years of the striving of the ignorant.
«29»- dh, Rawdat al-Wa'izin: The Prophet — may God bless him and his family — said: A man's mainstay is his intellect; and there is no religion for one who has no intellect.

Al-batir: the cutting. He likened forbearance to a covering veil because forbearance prevents the appearance of the base traits of character that anger entails. And he likened the intellect to a cutting blade because by the intellect man slays his most hostile enemy, namely his caprice; and by it he prevails over his soul, and holds it back from gaining mastery over the kingdom of the body, and prevents it from doing what harms its state.

Chapter 2: The reality of the intellect, its nature, and the beginning of its creation

«10»- 'a, 'Ilal al-Shara'i': my father, from Sa'd, from Ibn Hashim, from Ibn Ma'bad (1), from al-Husayn b. Khalid, from Ishaq, who said: I said to Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him: There is the man I come to and speak to with part of my speech, and he understands the whole of it; and among them is one I come to and speak to with the speech, and he takes in the whole of my speech and then repeats it back to me as I spoke it; and among them is one I come to and speak to, and he says: Repeat it to me. He said: Ishaq, do you not know why this is? I said: No. He said: The one you speak to with part of your speech and he understands the whole of it — that is one whose seed was kneaded with his intellect. As for the one you speak to and he takes in your speech and then answers you upon your speech — that is one whose intellect was compounded in him in his mother's belly. And as for the one you speak to with the speech and he says: Repeat it to me — that is one whose intellect was compounded in him after he had grown up; and so he says: Repeat it to me.

Elucidation: His words "then repeats it back to me" — that is, the substance of the speech as he heard it, or he answers in accordance with what I spoke to him; and the second is the more evident. Then know that it is possible that the speech runs by way of metaphor, to set out the difference of souls in their essential preparednesses — that is, it is as though his seed were kneaded with his intellect, for example. And it is possible that what is meant
In one copy: from Ibn Sa'id.

98.text: is that some people perfect their rational soul with intellect and with the preparedness to understand things and to perceive good and evil while it is a seed; and some of them while it is in the belly; and some of them after the person has grown up and used the senses and acquired the self-evident truths and the experience of affairs. And it is possible that what is meant is to point to the fact that the difference of bodily materials has a part in the difference of intellect. And God knows.

«11»- khts, al-Ikhtisas: al-Sadiq, peace be upon him, said: God, blessed and exalted, when He created the intellect, said to it: Come forward — and it came forward. Then He said to it: Go back — and it went back. Then He said: By My might and My majesty, I have not created a creature dearer to Me than you. By you I support whomever I love.

«12»- And he, peace be upon him, said: God created the intellect from four things: from knowledge, from power, from light (1) and from will by command. So He made it subsisting by knowledge, everlasting in the realm of dominion.

«13»- 'a, 'Ilal al-Shara'i': Ibn al-Walid, from al-Saffar, from Ibn 'Isa, from al-Bazanti, from Abu Jamila, from one he named, from Abu Ja'far, peace be upon him, who said: Harshness is in the liver, modesty is in the wind, and the intellect — its dwelling is the heart.

Elucidation: "Harshness is in the liver" — that is, it arises from some of the humours generated from the liver, such as blood and yellow bile, for example. And "the wind" is much used in the reports, as will come in the Book of the States of Man. From some of them it appears that it is the black bile; from some, that it is the animal spirit; and from some, that it is one of the parts of the body other than the four humours and the known parts. And "the heart" is applied to the human soul, on account of its attaching first to the animal spirit that issues from the pine-shaped heart; and for that reason

Perhaps what is meant by light is the manifestation of perfections, of noble characters and of pleasing deeds; and by will by command, the choosing of the fair among affairs.
