So the creation of the intellect from these things is perhaps a figure for its entailing them, as though they were its matter. And it is possible that min is causal — that is, He created it for the acquiring of those matters. Or the meaning is that He, exalted be He, did not create it from a matter, but created it from His knowledge, His power, His luminosity and His will, so that those effects appeared in it from the lights of His majesty. And what is meant is that the intellect is applied to the state composed of those qualities. As for its subsisting by knowledge, that is evident, since by the abandoning of knowledge the intellect is stripped away. And its being everlasting in the realm of dominion — since it is ever turned towards ascent to the highest degree, averted from the preoccupations of the world, joined to the spirits of those brought near in the highest assembly, and made ready for the ascent to the Garden of Refuge. From him, may his resting place be made sweet.

99.text: its attachment to the heart is greater than to the rest of the limbs; or on account of the turning about of its states. And the detailed discussion of this report will come in the Book of the Heaven and the World.

«14»- 'a, 'Ilal al-Shara'i', by his 'Alawi chain, from 'Ali b. Abi Talib, peace be upon them both, that the Prophet — may God bless him and his family — was asked: From what did God, Almighty and Glorious, create the intellect? He said: Its creation is an angel having heads to the number of the created beings — those who have been created and those who will be created until the Day of Resurrection. Every head has a face, and every human being has a head among the heads of the intellect, and the name of that person is written upon the face of that head. Upon every face is a veil cast down; and that veil is not lifted from that face until this child is born and reaches the limit of men or the limit of women. And when he reaches it, that veil is lifted, and a light falls into the heart of this person, so that he understands the obligation and the practice, the good and the bad. Indeed, the likeness of the intellect in the heart is as the likeness of the lamp in the middle of the house.

An extended discourse to clarify an intent: Know that the understanding of the reports of the chapters on the intellect depends upon an exposition of the quiddity of the intellect and of the differing opinions and technical usages concerning it. So we say: the intellect, in the root of the language, is the intellecting of things and the understanding of them; and its application has been technically fixed upon several matters. The first: it is the power of perceiving good and evil and of distinguishing between them, and the capacity to know the causes of things and the things possessed of causes, and what leads to them and what prevents them. And the intellect in this sense is the criterion of legal obligation, of reward and of punishment.

The second: a settled disposition and state in the soul that calls to the choosing of good and benefit and the avoiding of evils and harms; and by it the soul is strengthened to restrain the promptings of appetite and of anger and the whisperings of Satan. And is this the complete degree of the first, or is it another attribute and a state distinct from the first? Both are possible. And what is observed in most people — their judging some matters to be good while not performing them, and some matters to be evil while being addicted to them — indicates that this state is other than the knowledge of good and evil.

100.text: And what (1) has appeared to us from following the reports ascribed to the righteous Imams, God's peace be upon them, is that God has created in every one of the persons subject to obligation a power and a preparedness to perceive matters — harms, benefits and other things — with much difference between them in it. The least of its degrees is the criterion of obligation, and by it he is distinguished from the insane; and by the difference of its degrees the obligations vary. So the more complete this power is, the more burdensome and the more numerous the obligations. And this power is perfected in each person, according to his preparedness, by knowledge and by action; so whenever he strives to acquire what benefits him of the true sciences and acts by them, that power is strengthened. Then the sciences vary in the degrees of deficiency and of perfection; and whenever it increases in strength its effects become more numerous, and it urges its possessor, according to its strength, to act by them. For most people, their knowledge of the Origin and the Return and the rest of the pillars of faith is a conceptual knowledge which they call assent; and in some of them it is a conjectural assent; and in some of them a compelled assent. For that reason they do not act by what they claim. But when knowledge is perfected and reaches the degree of certainty, its effects appear upon its possessor at every moment. And the complete verification of that will come in the Book of Faith and Unbelief, if God the Exalted wills.

The third: the power which people employ in the ordering of the affairs of their livelihood. If it accords with the canon of the sacred law and is employed in what the Lawgiver has approved, it is called the intellect of livelihood, and it is praised in the reports; and its distinctness from what has passed is by a kind of consideration. And when it is employed in false matters and corrupt stratagems, it is called cunning and devilry in the tongue of the sacred law. And some have posited another power for that, which is not established.

What he mentions, may God have mercy on him, of the meanings of the intellect, claiming that they are the technical usages for the meanings of the intellect, applies only to what the people of investigation have technically fixed upon; and not to what the generality of people other than them hold — as is not hidden from one expert and versed in these investigations. And what led him into what he fell into are two things. The first: ill opinion of those who investigate the intellectual sciences by way of reason and demonstration. The second: the way he followed in understanding the meanings of the reports, in that he took them all at a single level of exposition — namely the one that general understandings attain, which is the level at which most of the reports answering the questions of the majority of those who questioned them, peace be upon them, were sent down; whereas among the reports are choice ones pointing to realities that none attain but lofty understandings and pure intellects. So that brought about the confusion of the divine sciences flowing from them, peace be upon them, and the spoiling of the lofty expositions by bringing them down to a level that is not theirs, and the spoiling of the simple expositions too, by their losing their distinctness and their definiteness. For not every questioner among the transmitters is at one level of understanding, nor is every reality at one level of subtlety and delicacy. And the Book and the Sunna are filled with the fact that the divine sciences of the religion have differing degrees, that each degree has its own people, and that in the cancelling of the degrees lies the destruction of the true sciences. T.

101.text: The fourth: the degrees of the soul's preparedness for the acquiring of theoretical knowledge, and its nearness to and distance from that. They have posited for it four degrees, which they have named the material intellect, the intellect in the mode of disposition, the intellect in act, and the acquired intellect. These names are sometimes applied to the soul in those degrees. Their detailed account is set down in its own places, and it comes back to what we mentioned first; for it appears that it is a single power whose names differ according to its objects and to what it is employed in.
The fifth: the human rational soul, by which man is distinguished from the rest of the beasts.

The sixth: what the philosophers have held to and, in their claim, established — an immaterial, pre-eternal substance having no connection with matter either in essence or in act. Holding to it as they have stated it entails the denial of many of the necessary tenets of religion, such as the temporal origination of the world and other matters this place does not admit of mentioning. And some of them who profess Islam have posited originated intellects; and these too, as they have posited them, entail the denial of many of the established Islamic principles — quite apart from the fact that there does not appear from the reports the existence of any immaterial being other than God the Exalted.

And some of their verifiers said that the relation of the tenth intellect, which they call the active intellect, to the soul is as the relation of the soul to the body: so just as the soul is a form for the body and the body is its matter, likewise the intellect is a form for the soul and the soul is its matter; and it shines upon it, and its sciences are derived from it; and this connection is perfected to the point that the sciences are read off in it and it is joined to it. And they have no proof for these matters save specious ambiguities or strange fancies which they have adorned with subtle expressions.

Now that you know what we have laid down, know that most of the reports that have come down in these chapters are apparent in the first two senses, whose issue comes back to one; and in the second of the two more so and more evidently. And some of the reports admit of some of the other senses; and in some of the reports the intellect is applied to beneficial knowledge itself — that which bequeaths deliverance and entails the attaining of felicities.

As for the reports of the intellect's being made to speak, and of its coming forward and its going back: it is possible to construe them upon one of the four senses mentioned first, or upon what comprises them all. And in that case it is possible that creation is in the sense of determining, as has come in the language; or that what is meant by creation is creation in the soul and the soul's being qualified by it, and that the rest of what is mentioned in them — the making to speak, the coming forward, the going back and the like — is a representational metaphor to set out

102.text: that the pivot of obligations, of perfections and of ascents is the intellect. And it is possible that what is meant by the making to speak is His rendering it capable of perceiving the sciences by it, and that the command to come forward and to go back is a creative command rendering it capable of being a means for the acquiring of this world and the next, of felicity and of wretchedness alike, and an instrument to be employed in coming to know the realities of things and in reflecting upon the subtleties of stratagems as well.
And in some of the reports: By you I command, and by you I forbid, and by you I punish, and by you I reward.

And this fits this sense, because the least of its degrees is the criterion of the validity of the principle of obligation, and every degree of its degrees is the criterion of the validity of some of the obligations. And in some of the reports "you it is" stands in place of "by you" in every position, and in some of them in some positions. So what is meant is emphasis upon obligation's being conditional upon it, as though it were in reality the one obligated. And as for what is in some of the reports, that it is the first creature among the spiritual beings — it is possible that what is meant is the first determined of the attributes pertaining to the spirit, or the first innate disposition upon which the soul is imprinted and which is deposited in it; or its priority may be by reason of the priority of the souls to which it pertains. And as for when they are construed upon the fifth sense, it is possible that this too is by way of representation, as has passed. Its being created is evident; and its being the first created is either by reason of the souls' having been created before the bodies, as has come in reports widely transmitted — so it is possible that the creation of the spirits preceded the creation of all created things besides them. But the report "the first thing God created was the intellect" I have not found in the reliable reports; it is only taken from the reports of the wider community. And the apparent sense of most of our reports is that the first of created things is water or air, as will come in the Book of the Heaven and the World. Yes, it has come in our reports that the intellect is the first creature among the spiritual beings; and that does not conflict with the precedence of the creation of some bodies over its creation. And in that case what is meant by its coming forward — upon what a group has held concerning the immateriality of the soul — is its turning towards the world of immaterial beings, and by its going back its attachment to the body and to material things. Or what is meant by its coming forward is its turning towards the lofty stations and the exalted degrees, and by its going back its descent from those stations and its turning to the acquiring of base worldly matters and its likening itself to beasts and animals. So upon what we have mentioned of representation, the purpose is to set out that it has these differing preparednesses and these far-separated conditions. And if we do not construe it upon representation, it is possible that the making to speak is real, and that it is a figure for His rendering it a perceiver of universals; and likewise the command to come forward and to go back

103.text: may be real, on account of the evidentness of its submission to what He, exalted be He, wills of it; and it may be a creative command, that it may be capable of the two things — that is, ascent to perfection, to nearness and to union, and descent to deficiency and to what entails ruin; or that it may be at an intermediate degree of immateriality on account of its attachment to material things. But the immateriality of the soul has not been established for us from the reports; rather what appears from them is its materiality, as we shall explain hereafter, if God the Exalted wills.

As for the sixth sense: if someone were to hold to an immaterial substance without holding to its pre-eternity, and without making the acting of the Necessary Being upon contingent things depend upon it, nor holding to its acting in the creation of things, and were to name it the intellect and make some of those reports fit what he has named intellect — then he could say that its coming forward is an expression of its turning towards the Origin, and its going back an expression of its turning towards the souls, on account of its shining upon them and their perfecting themselves by it.
Now that you know that, listen to what is recited to you of the truth that deserves to be set forth, and that no heed be paid to what the deficient among minds recoil from.

So know that most of what they have established for these intellects has been established for the spirits of the Prophet and the Imams, peace be upon them, in our widely transmitted reports, in another manner. For they established pre-eternity for the intellect; and precedence in creation has been established for their spirits — either over all created things or over the rest of the spiritual beings — in widely transmitted reports. And likewise they established for them mediation in bringing into existence, or conditionality in acting; and it has been established in the reports that they, peace be upon them, are the final cause of all created things, and that but for them God would not have created the celestial spheres and the rest. And they established for them their being intermediaries in the effusion of sciences and of divine knowledge upon the souls and the spirits; and it has been established in the reports that all sciences, realities and divine knowledge are effused upon the rest of creation — even the angels and the prophets — through their mediation.

The upshot is that it has been established by widely transmitted reports that they, peace be upon them, are the means between creation and the Truth in the effusion of all mercies, sciences and perfections upon all creation. So the more the seeking of recourse through them and the acknowledgement of their excellence, the greater the effusion of perfections from God. And since they travelled the path of spiritual exercises and reflections, relying independently upon their own opinions and not upon the canon of the sacred law, the reality of this matter appeared to them confusedly and ambiguously; so they erred in that, and posited intellects, and spoke concerning

104.text: that superfluously (1). So upon the analogy of what they said, it is possible that what is meant by the intellect is the light of the Prophet — may God bless him and his family — from which the lights of the Imams, peace be upon them, branched off; and its being made to speak in reality, or by His making it a locus for unbounded divine knowledge. And what is meant by the command to come forward is his ascent through the degrees of perfection and his being drawn to the highest station of nearness and union; and by his going back, either his descent to the body, or the command to perfect creation after the utmost of perfection — for that entails a descent from the utmost degrees of nearness by reason of associating with creation. And His words, exalted be He, point to it: "God has sent down to you a remembrance, a messenger" (2). And we have set out the discussion of that at length in al-Fawa'id al-Tarifa. And it is possible that what is meant by the coming forward is the coming forward to creation, and by the going back the return to the world of holiness after the completion of the delivering of the message; and what is in some of the reports of the placing of the going back before the coming forward supports it. And on all suppositions, as for His words, exalted be He, "and I shall not perfect you" — it is possible that what is meant is: and I shall not perfect my love for you, and the connection with you, and your being an intermediary between Him and me, save in one whom I love. Or the address is with their spirit and their light, peace be upon them; and what is meant by the perfecting is its perfecting in their noble bodies — that is, this light, after its branching, in whatever body it attaches and is perfected, that person is the most beloved of creation to God the Exalted. And His words "you it is

Rather it is because they established, first, that the religious apparent senses depend for their probative force upon the demonstration which the intellect sets up; and the intellect, in its resting and its assurance upon demonstrative premises, does not distinguish between one premise and another — so when a demonstration is established for a thing, the intellect is compelled to accept it. And second, that the religious apparent senses depend upon the apparent sense of the wording, which is a conjectural indication; and conjecture cannot withstand the knowledge attained by demonstration, should demonstration be established for a thing. As for taking demonstrations in the principles of religion and then dismissing the intellect in what has come in single reports of the intellectual sciences — that is nothing but of the sort of invalidating a premise by the conclusion drawn from it, which is plain contradiction; and God is the Guide. For if these religious apparent senses were to invalidate the judgement of the intellect, they would first invalidate their own judgement, whose probative force rests upon the judgement of the intellect. And the path of religious caution, for one who is not firmly grounded in the deep intellectual investigations, is to hold to the apparent sense of the Book and to the apparent senses of the widely transmitted reports, and to refer the knowledge of their realities to God, exalted be His name, and to avoid entering into the deep intellectual investigations, whether affirming or denying: affirming, because it is a likely place of error and holds an exposure to everlasting perdition; and denying, because of the evil consequence in it of speaking without knowledge, and of aiding the religion by what God, glory be to Him, is not pleased with, and of being afflicted with self-contradiction in reasoning. And take a lesson in that from what the author, may God have mercy on him, was afflicted with: for he did not impugn the opinions of the people of speculation in the discussions of the Origin and the Return in any point but that he was afflicted with holding to the very same thing, or to something more extreme, as we shall point out in its places. The first of that is what is in this question: for he impugned the philosophers in it for their holding to immaterial beings, and then established all the properties of immateriality for the lights of the Prophet and the Imams, peace be upon them — and he did not notice that if the existence of an immaterial existent other than God, glory be to Him, were impossible, the judgement of its impossibility would not be altered by altering its name, and by naming what they call intellect "light", "clay" and the like. T.

105.text: that I command" — the singling out is either because they, God's blessings be upon them, are obligated with what others are not obligated with, and there proceeds from them of the due of His worship, exalted be He, what does not proceed from others; or because the validity of the deeds of the servants is conditional upon allegiance to them and acknowledgement of their excellence, in the manner of the figurative usage that has passed. And by this verification it is possible to reconcile
what has been related from the Prophet — may God bless him and his family — The first thing God created was my light
what has been related: The first thing God created was the intellect.
And what has been related: The first thing God created was the light.

if their chains are sound. And the verification of this discourse as it ought to be requires a kind of expansion and prolixity; and were we to render it its due, we should have broken what we promised at the head of the book.

As for the last report, it is among the obscure of the reports; and it appears that the discourse in it is cast in the manner of symbols and secrets. It is possible that it is a figure for its attaching to every person subject to obligation, and that that attachment has a particular time, and that before that time there are impediments to the attachment of the intellect — of dark coverings and material turbidities — like a veil let down over the face of the intellect. And it is possible to construe it upon the apparent sense of its reality, upon some of the foregoing possibilities. And his words "its creation is an angel" — perhaps it is by way of annexation, that is, its constitution is like the constitution of the angels in its subtlety and its spirituality. And it is possible that "its creation" is annexed to the pronoun as a subject and "an angel" is its predicate — that is, its constitution is the constitution of an angel; or it is an angel in reality. And God knows.
Chapter 3: God's argument against mankind by way of the intellect, and that He calls them to account according to their intellects

«1»- j, al-Ihtijaj, in the report of Ibn al-Sikkit (1). He said: Then what is the proof against creation today? Al-Rida, peace be upon him, said: The intellect. By it you know the one truthful about God, and so believe him; and the one lying about God, and so disbelieve him. Ibn al-Sikkit said: This, by God, is the answer.
'a, 'Ilal al-Shara'i'; n, 'Uyun Akhbar al-Rida, peace be upon him: Ibn Masrur, from Ibn 'Amir, from Abu 'Abd Allah al-Sayyari, from Abu Ya'qub al-Baghdadi (2), from Ibn al-Sikkit, the like of it (3).
He is the Imami, trustworthy, firmly reliable traditionist, the leading authority in lexicography, pre-eminent in letters. Al-Mutawakkil the 'Abbasid killed him for his Shi'ism.

He is Yazid b. Hammad al-Anbari al-Sulami, Abu Ya'qub the secretary. Al-Shaykh set him down in the chapter of the companions of al-Rida, peace be upon him, in his Rijal, and declared him trustworthy, and his father Hammad likewise. Al-'Allama gave his entry in the first section of al-Khulasa and declared him trustworthy, and so did everyone who came after the two of them.
He related it in al-Kafi in the Book of Intellect and Ignorance with an addition; and there will come from us a discussion concerning the tradition.

106.text: «2»- m', Ma'ani al-Akhbar: my father, from 'Ali b. Ibrahim, from Muhammad b. 'Isa, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Yazid al-Razzaz, from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, who said: Abu Ja'far, peace be upon him, said: My son, know the ranks of the Shi'a according to the measure of their narration and their knowledge; for knowledge is the discernment of the narration, and by discernments of narrations the believer rises to the furthest degrees of faith. I looked into a book of 'Ali, peace be upon him, and found in the book that the worth of every man and his measure is his knowledge. God, blessed and exalted, calls people to account according to the measure of what He has given them of intellects in the abode of this world.

«3»- sn, al-Mahasin: al-Husayn b. 'Ali b. Yaqtin, from Muhammad b. Sinan, from Abu al-Jarud, from Abu Ja'far, peace be upon him, who said: God is exacting with the servants in the reckoning on the Day of Resurrection only according to the measure of what He has given them of intellects in this world.

«4»- sn, al-Mahasin: Muhammad al-Barqi, from Sulayman b. Ja'far al-Ja'fari, raising it, said: The Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: We, the company of prophets, speak to people according to the measure of their intellects.

«5»- sn, al-Mahasin: al-Nawfali and Jahm b. Hakim al-Mada'ini, from al-Sakuni, from Abu 'Abd Allah, from his forefathers, peace be upon them, who said: The Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: When there reaches you concerning a man the goodness of his state (1), look into the goodness of his intellect; for he is recompensed only according to his intellect.
Chapter 4: The signs of the intellect and its hosts

«1»- l, al-Khisal: my father, from Sa'd, from al-Barqi, from his father, raising it, said: The Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: The intellect is apportioned into three parts. Whoever has them in him, his intellect is complete; and whoever does not have them in him has no intellect: goodness of knowledge of God, Almighty and Glorious; goodness of obedience to Him; and goodness of patience upon His command.
Elucidation: perhaps the counting of these things — which are among the effects of the intellect — as its parts is by way of hyperbole

Of the performance of prayer, fasting, the pilgrimage, the giving of alms and charities, and other rewarded acts and means of nearness. And his words "look into the goodness of his intellect" — that is, if you see his intellect to be complete, infer from it the goodness of his acts and the soundness of his deeds, and that he is worthy to be relied upon and depended upon; and if you see it to be deficient, be not deceived by his deeds nor rely upon him, and infer from the smallness of his intellect the deficiency of his reward — for he is recompensed and rewarded according to the measure of his intellect in completeness and in deficiency.

107.text: and expansion and figurative usage, on account of the connection of their not being separable from it and of their indicating it.

«2»- l, al-Khisal: Majilawayh, from Muhammad al-'Attar, from Muhammad b. Ahmad, from Sahl, from Ja'far b. Muhammad b. Bashshar, from al-Dihqan, from Durust (1), from 'Abd al-A'la, from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, who said: A man's intellect is judged in three things: in the length of his beard, in the engraving of his signet-ring, and in his agnomen.

«3»- 'a, 'Ilal al-Shara'i'; l, al-Khisal: Ahmad b. Muhammad b. 'Abd al-Rahman al-Marwazi, from Muhammad b. Ja'far al-Muqri' al-Jurjani, from Muhammad b. al-Hasan al-Mawsili, from Muhammad b. 'Asim al-Tarifi, from 'Ayyash b. Yazid b. al-Hasan b. 'Ali al-Kahhal, client of Zayd b. 'Ali, from his father, from Musa b. Ja'far, from his father Ja'far b. Muhammad, from his father Muhammad b. 'Ali, from his father 'Ali b. al-Husayn, from his father al-Husayn b. 'Ali, from his father the Commander of the Faithful 'Ali b. Abi Talib, peace be upon them both, who said: The Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: God created the intellect from a light stored and hidden in His foreknowledge, which no sent prophet and no angel brought near has looked upon. He made knowledge its self, understanding its spirit, abstinence its head, modesty its two eyes, wisdom its tongue, compassion its concern, and mercy its heart. Then He filled it out and strengthened it with ten things: with certainty, faith, truthfulness, tranquillity, sincerity, gentleness, giving, contentment, submission and gratitude. Then He, Almighty and Glorious, said: Go back — and it went back. Then He said to it: Come forward — and it came forward. Then He said to it: Speak. It said: Praise be to God, who has no opposite and no equal, no likeness and no peer and no match and no similitude; He before whose greatness everything is submissive and lowly. So the Lord, blessed and exalted, said: By My might and My majesty, I have not created a creature fairer than you, nor more obedient to Me than you, nor higher than you, nor nobler than you, nor dearer than you. By you I am declared one, and by you I am worshipped, and by you I am called upon, and by you I am hoped in, and by you I am sought, and by you I am feared, and by you caution is taken, and by you is the reward, and by you is the punishment. So the intellect at that fell down prostrate, and it was in its prostration a thousand years. Then the Lord, blessed and exalted, said: Raise your head, and ask and you shall be given, and intercede and your intercession shall be accepted. So the intellect raised its head and said: My God, I ask You to accept my intercession for the one in whom You created me. So God, majestic be His majesty, said to His angels: I call you to witness that I have accepted its intercession for the one in whom I created it.
Elucidation: there has already passed what may be employed in the understanding of this report. And light is what becomes a cause of the appearance of
With damma on the dal and the ra' and sukun on the sin. Al-Najashi gave his entry in his book, p. 117.

108.text: a thing; and the intellect is among His lights, exalted be He, which He created and determined for the disclosing of divine knowledge to creation — that is, He created it from a kind of light and from its stock, and its matter was a luminous thing stored in the treasuries of the Throne. And figurative usage is possible, as has passed. And knowledge, for the intensity of its connection with it and its being its most excellent benefit and that which perfects it to the highest degree — it is as though it were its self and its very being; and it, without understanding, is like a body without a spirit. "And abstinence its head" — that is, the most excellent of its virtues and the highest of them, just as the head is the noblest of the parts of the body; or it is annulled by the annulment of abstinence, just as the person dies by the parting of the head. And modesty is a help towards the disclosing of the true matters to it, or to whoever is qualified by it — like the two eyes. And wisdom is the interpreter of the intellect, as the tongue is for the person. And mercy is a cause of the effusion of realities upon it from God, and a way for them — like the heart. And its prostration is either a figure for its surrender and for the submission of the one qualified by it to the Truth, exalted be He; or what is meant is the prostration of one of those qualified by it. And it is not hidden that most of the parts of this report fit the last sense — that is, the lights of the Imams, peace be upon them; and figurative usage, representation and likening is perhaps the more evident. And it is said shaffa'tuhu fi kadha, that is, I accepted his intercession in it. And the explanation of some of the parts will come in the report that follows.

«4»- l, al-Khisal: my father, from Sa'd, from Ahmad b. Hilal, from Umayya b. 'Ali, from Ibn al-Mughira, from Ibn Khalid, from Abu Ja'far, peace be upon him, who said: The Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: God, Almighty and Glorious, has not been worshipped with anything more excellent than the intellect. And the believer is not possessed of intellect until ten qualities are gathered in him: good is hoped for from him and evil is safe from him; he reckons much the little good from another and reckons little the much good from himself; he does not weary (1) of seeking knowledge all his life long; he is not vexed (2) by those who seek their needs from him; lowliness is more beloved to him than might, and poverty more beloved to him than wealth; his portion of the world is bare sustenance. And the tenth: he sees no one but that he says: He is better than I and more God-fearing. For people are but two men: a man who is better than he and more God-fearing, and another who is worse than he and lower. So when he sees one who is better than he and more God-fearing, he humbles himself before him that he may join him; and when he meets one who is worse than he and lower, he says: Perhaps this man's good is inward and his evil outward, and perhaps his end will be sealed with good. And when he does that, his glory has risen high and he has become the chief of the people of his age.
That is, he does not grow weary nor become vexed.
That is, he does not become vexed.

109.text: «5»- ma, the Amali of al-Shaykh al-Tusi: al-Mufid, from Muhammad b. 'Umar al-Ju'abi, from Ahmad b. Muhammad b. Sa'id, from al-Hasan b. Ja'far, from Tahir b. Midrar, from Zurr [Razin b. Anas], who said: I heard Ja'far b. Muhammad, peace be upon them both, saying: The believer is not a believer until he is complete in intellect; and he is not complete in intellect until ten qualities are in him. And he carried the tradition on in the manner of what has passed.

«6»- 'a, 'Ilal al-Shara'i': Ibn al-Walid, from al-Saffar, from Ibrahim b. Hashim, from Abu Ishaq Ibrahim b. al-Haytham al-Khaffaf, from a man of our companions, from 'Abd al-Malik b. Hisham, from 'Ali al-Ash'ari, raising it, said: The Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: God has not been worshipped with the like of the intellect; and no man's intellect has been complete until ten qualities are in him. And he mentioned the like of it.

Elucidation: in ma and 'a, after his words "and the tenth" is "and what is the tenth?" And his words, peace be upon him, "God has not been worshipped with anything" — that is, nothing becomes a cause of worship, and an instrument for it, and a perfecter of it, like the intellect. And it is possible that what is meant by the intellect is the intellecting of religious matters and of the certain divine sciences, and reflection upon them, and the acquiring of knowledge — and that is among the most excellent acts of worship, as will come; so what is mentioned after it would be of the attributes of the learned. And al-majd is the attaining of honour and nobility. And "he has become chief of the people of his age" — that is, he became their master, their great one and their noblest.

«7»- l, al-Khisal: my father, from Sa'd and al-Himyari together, from al-Barqi, from 'Ali b. Hadid, from Sama'a, who said: I was with Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, and with him was a company of his followers, and the mention of intellect and ignorance came up. So Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, said: Know the intellect and its host, and ignorance and its host, and you will be rightly guided. Sama'a said: So I said: May I be made your ransom, we know only what you have made known to us. So Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, said: God, majestic be His praise, created the intellect — and it is the first creature He created among the spiritual beings (1) — on the right of the Throne, from His light (2). He said to it: Come forward — and it came forward. Then He said to it: Go back — and it went back. So God, blessed and exalted, said: I have created you a great creation and honoured you above all My creation. He said: Then He created ignorance from the bitter sea, dark; and He said

Al-ruh, with damma on the ra', is applied in the Qur'an and in the hadith to several senses: among them Gabriel, the Holy Spirit and the rest of the angels; among them that by which the body subsists and by which life is; among them the human rational power; and it is applied to the intellect also. In the relative adjective of the singular you say al-ruhani, and of the plural al-ruhaniyyun, the alif and the nun being among the additions of the relative form. And the world of immaterial beings, the world of dominion and the world of the command are called al-ruhaniyyun.
Perhaps it is a pointer to the intellect's not being composed of dark matter. And the annexation to Him, exalted be He, is honorific.

110.text: to it: Go back — and it went back. Then He said to it: Come forward — and it did not come forward. So He said to it: You have grown proud. And He cursed it. Then He appointed for the intellect seventy-five hosts. And when ignorance saw what God had honoured the intellect with and what He had given it, it concealed enmity towards it. So ignorance (1) said: My Lord, this is a creature like me; You created it and honoured it and strengthened it, and I am its opposite and have no strength against it. So give me of the host the like of what You have given it. He said: Yes; but if you disobey (2) after that, I shall drive you and your host out of My mercy. It said: I am content. So He gave it seventy-five hosts. And among what He gave the intellect of the seventy-five hosts was good, and it is the vizier of the intellect; and He made its opposite evil, and it is the vizier of ignorance. And faith, and its opposite unbelief; and assent, and its opposite denial; and hope (3), and its opposite despondency; and justice, and its opposite injustice; and contentment, and its opposite displeasure; and gratitude, and its opposite ingratitude; and expectation, and its opposite despair; and trust, and its opposite covetousness; and compassion, and its opposite heedlessness; and mercy, and its opposite wrath; and knowledge, and its opposite ignorance; and understanding, and its opposite folly; and chastity, and its opposite shamelessness; and abstinence, and its opposite desire; and gentleness, and its opposite roughness; and awe, and its opposite boldness; and humility, and its opposite arrogance; and deliberateness, and its opposite haste; and forbearance, and its opposite foolishness; and silence, and its opposite babbling; and submission, and its opposite haughtiness; and surrender, and its opposite tyranny; and pardon, and its opposite rancour; and tenderness, and its opposite hardness; and certainty, and its opposite doubt; and patience, and its opposite anxiety; and overlooking, and its opposite vengeance; and sufficiency, and its opposite poverty (4); and reflection, and its opposite inadvertence; and retention, and its opposite forgetfulness; and affection, and its opposite severance; and contentment, and its opposite greed; and mutual sharing, and its opposite withholding; and love, and its opposite enmity; and fidelity, and its opposite treachery; and obedience, and its opposite disobedience; and submissiveness, and its opposite overbearing; and safety, and its opposite affliction; and loving, and its opposite hating; and truthfulness, and its opposite lying; and truth, and its opposite falsehood; and trustworthiness, and its opposite betrayal; and sincerity, and its opposite

Perhaps what is meant by ignorance is the soul that commands to evil, and the appetites which are the origin of every fault — not the ignorance opposed to knowledge, for that is among its hosts, as comes in the tradition. And the application of ignorance to the soul comes in tradition 11.

Hope for God's mercy and the absence of despair of His forgiveness for what he has neglected of his duty towards Him, exalted be He; and its counterpart is despair of His mercy and His forgiveness, and that is greater than his sin and his fault.

111.text: adulteration (1); and sagacity, and its opposite dullness (2); and understanding, and its opposite obtuseness (3); and knowing, and its opposite disavowal; and forbearing courtesy, and its opposite open contention; and soundness in absence, and its opposite guile; and concealment, and its opposite divulging; and prayer, and its opposite the neglecting of it; and fasting, and its opposite the breaking of the fast; and struggle, and its opposite shrinking back; and the pilgrimage, and its opposite the casting away of the covenant; and the guarding of speech, and its opposite talebearing; and dutifulness to parents, and its opposite disobedience to them; and genuineness, and its opposite ostentation; and the good, and its opposite the reprehensible; and covering, and its opposite flaunting; and prudent concealment, and its opposite broadcasting; and equity, and its opposite partisanship; and service, and its opposite insolence; and cleanliness (4), and its opposite filth; and modesty, and its opposite the casting off of it; and moderation, and its opposite transgression; and rest, and its opposite toil; and ease, and its opposite difficulty; and blessing, and its opposite blighting; and well-being, and its opposite affliction; and sufficiency of means, and its opposite the vying for more; and wisdom, and its opposite caprice; and dignity, and its opposite levity; and felicity, and its opposite wretchedness (5); and repentance, and its opposite persistence; and the seeking of forgiveness, and its opposite self-deception; and vigilance, and its opposite carelessness; and supplication, and its opposite the disdaining of it; and briskness (6), and its opposite sloth; and gladness, and its opposite sorrow; and fellowship, and its opposite separation; and open-handedness, and its opposite miserliness. So these qualities, all of them among the hosts of the intellect, are not gathered save in a prophet, or the legatee of a prophet, or a believer whose heart God has tested for faith. As for the rest of that among our followers — one of them does not fail to have in him some of these hosts, until he becomes complete and guards against the hosts of ignorance; and at that point he is in the highest degree, with the prophets and the legatees, peace be upon them. And triumph is attained only by the knowing of the intellect and its hosts and by the shunning of ignorance and its hosts. May God grant us and you success in obeying Him and in what pleases Him.
'a, 'Ilal al-Shara'i': Ibn al-Walid, from al-Saffar, from al-Barqi, from 'Ali b. Hadid, from Sama'a, the like of it. — sn, al-Mahasin: from 'Ali b. Hadid, the like of it.
With fatha on the ba': the absence of keenness and acuteness.
With fatha on the dotted ghayn: ignorance and little acuteness.
Because the observing of it bequeaths soundness in the soul and draws people to him; and filth bequeaths sickness and disease and makes people shun him.
In the obedience of God and in His worship, or in what is more general than that and than the acquiring of lawful wealth.

112.text: Elucidation: what is mentioned of the hosts here is eighty-one qualities, and in al-Kafi seventy-eight; and it seems to be on account of the repetition of some of the clauses, either from him, peace be upon him, or from the copyists, in that they added some of the copies to the original. And the intellect here admits of the foregoing senses; and ignorance is either the power that calls to evil, or the body, if what is meant by the intellect is the soul. And Iblis is also possible, because he is the one who opposes the possessors of complete intellects among the prophets and the Imams in the guidance of creation; and what supports it is that the like of this has come concerning the opposition of Adam and Iblis after his rebellion, and that He gave the two of them the like of those hosts. The upshot is that these are hosts for the intellect and its people, and those are armies for ignorance and its masters. Good is its being conducive to good things, or to the conveying of good either to itself or to another; and evil is its counterpart in the two senses. And He named the two of them viziers because they are the sources of all that is mentioned after them of the hosts; so they are two commanders over them, strengthening them, and all of them issue from their judgement. And assent and denial are perhaps among the repeated clauses. It is possible to specify faith to what pertains to the principles and assent to what pertains to the derivative rulings; and it is possible that the distinction is by summary and detail, in that faith is summary assent to what the Prophet — may God bless him and his family — brought, and assent is acknowledgement of its details. And justice is the mean in all matters between excess and defect, or the well-known sense, which is included in the first. And contentment, that is, with God's decree. And expectation is perhaps a repetition of hope; and it is possible to specify hope to matters of the hereafter and expectation to worldly benefits, or hope to what is by desert and expectation to what is not; or what is meant by expectation is coveting what is in people's hands, so that it would be among the hosts of ignorance, set down contrary to the order — and its remoteness is not hidden.

And compassion and mercy — one of the two is among the repetitions; and it is possible that what is meant by compassion is the state and by mercy its fruit. And in al-Kafi and al-Mahasin the opposite of compassion is hardness; and in most copies of al-Khisal it is al-'izza, that is, the seeking of mastery and domination. And understanding — either what is meant by it is a state of the soul entailing swiftness in perceiving matters and knowledge of the subtleties of questions, or the principle of perception; so upon the second it is specified to practical wisdom, so as to differ from knowledge. And chastity is the restraining of the belly and the private parts from forbidden and doubtful things; and its counterpart is shamelessness and not caring about the rending of one's veil in committing forbidden things. And he said in al-Qamus: al-khurq, with damma and with the vowelling,

113.text: is the opposite of gentleness, and it is not doing work well nor managing affairs well. And awe is fear of God and of His punishment, or of creation, or of the soul and Satan; and the better course is to generalize it, so as to include fear of everything that harms religion or this world. And al-tu'ada, with damma on the ta' and fatha on the hamza or its quiescence, is gravity and deliberateness — that is, not rushing to matters without reflection, for that brings about falling into places of destruction. And in al-Qamus: hadhara his speech, on the pattern of fariha — it was much in error and falsehood; and al-hadhar, with the vowelling, is the much that is bad, or the worthless of speech.

And submission is compliance with God the Exalted in what He commands and forbids; and surrender is compliance with the Imams of truth. And in al-Kafi, opposite surrender is doubt; so what is meant by surrender is acknowledgement of what issues from the prophets and the Imams, peace be upon them, and which minds find hard to accept, as will come in the chapters on knowledge. And what is meant by sufficiency is the sufficiency of the soul and independence from creation — not sufficiency by wealth, for that is mostly with the people of ignorance; and its opposite is poverty towards people and the seeking of recourse to them in affairs. And since inadvertence is an expression of the disappearance of the form from the perceiving faculty and not from the retentive faculty, there was set opposite it recollection, which is the recovering from the retentive faculty. And since forgetfulness is an expression of its disappearance from the retentive faculty also, there was set opposite it retention. And mutual sharing is the making of one's brothers partakers and partners in wealth. And safety is freedom from afflictions, which are faults and blights; and the man of intellect escapes them, since he knows them and knows the way of escaping them, while the ignorant chooses them and falls into them from where he does not know. And al-Shaykh al-Baha'i, may God have mercy on him, said: perhaps what is meant is people's being safe from him,
as has come in the tradition: The Muslim is he from whose hand and tongue the Muslims are safe.
and what is meant by affliction is people's being afflicted by him. And sagacity is the keenness of the heart and its quickness.

His words, peace be upon him, "and understanding, and its opposite obtuseness" — in 'a: "acuteness, and its opposite obtuseness"; and perhaps that is preferable, for the absence of repetition. And upon what is in l, perhaps it is among the repetitions; and it is possible to specify one of the two to the understanding of the interests of the first world and the other to the next, or one of them to a degree of understanding and keenness and the other to a degree above it. And the distinction between it and sagacity also requires a forced construction. And knowing, according to what has been said, is the perceiving of a thing by its attributes and its traces, such that were he to come upon it he would know that it is it; and its counterpart is disavowal, meaning the non-attainment of that perception — for disavowal is applied to it also, as it is applied to

114.text: denial. And open contention is dispute and wrangling; and in sn: "forbearing courtesy, and its opposite harshness". And soundness in absence — that is, in his absence another is safe from his harm; and its opposite is guile, which is that he flatters outwardly for deceit and cunning, while in absence he is in the position of doing harm. And in sn: "soundness of heart, and its opposite guile"; and perhaps that is more fitting.

And concealment, that is, the concealing of the faults of the believers and their secrets, or of everything it is obligatory or fitting to conceal — such as the concealing of the truth in a position of prudent dissimulation, and the concealing of knowledge from those unfit for it. And prayer, that is, the guarding of it and of its proprieties and its times; and its opposite is the impairing of its conditions or its proprieties or the times of its excellence. And the casting away of the covenant — that is, its throwing off — was made the opposite of the pilgrimage only because of what will come in many reports, that God the Exalted deposited in the Stone the covenants of the servants, and that the reason for the pilgrimage is the renewal of the covenant at the Stone, so that it will bear witness on the Day of Resurrection for everyone who comes to it. And perhaps what is meant by genuineness is sincerity in worship, since by abandoning it the reality of worship is annulled; and this clause too is close to the clause of sincerity and adulteration. So either it is to be construed as repetition, or sincerity is to be construed upon its completeness — in that there is not mixed with it desire for the Garden nor fear of the Fire, nor the drawing of benefit nor the repelling of harm — and genuineness upon the absence of showing off before created beings. And the good, that is, choosing it and performing it and enjoining it; and likewise the reprehensible. And flaunting is the display of adornment; and perhaps this clause is particular to women, though it is possible to generalize it so as to include men's covering their nakedness and their faults. And broadcasting is divulging. And equity is evenness and justice between himself and another, and between near kin and those far off; and partisanship entails his preferring himself to another even if the other has the better right, and preferring his clan and his kin to those far off even if the right is with those far off. And al-mihna, with kasra and with fatha and with the vowelling, like kalima, is skill in service and in work: mahanahu, on the pattern of mana'ahu and nasarahu, mahnan and mihnatan — and it is also given with kasra — he served him, and he beat him, and he wore him out. Thus in al-Qamus. And what is meant is the service of the Imams of truth and obedience to them; and insolence is rising against them and not complying with them. And in al-Kafi and sn it is al-tahyi'a, and it has come in the sense of accord and setting right, and it comes back to what we have mentioned. And al-jal' in some copies is with jim, and it is little modesty; and in some of them with the dotted kha', that is, the casting off of the garment of modesty, and that is a widespread figure. And moderation is the choosing of the mean in affairs and the keeping to the middle path that leads to deliverance. And rest, that is, the choosing of what brings it about with respect to the two worlds, not the rest of this world only. And ease is compliance with ease and gentleness

115.text: of manner. And blessing comes in the sense of firmness, increase and growth — that is, firmness upon the truth, and striving in the increase of good deeds and in the growth of faith and certainty, and the leaving of what brings about the blighting of these matters, that is, their annulment, their diminution and their corruption. And it is possible that what is meant is blessing in wealth and in other worldly matters; for the man of intellect acquires from the quarter that is proper for him and spends upon what it is fitting to spend upon, so it grows and increases and remains and endures for him — unlike the ignorant. And well-being from sins and faults, or from things disliked; for the man of intellect, by gratitude and by pardon, ties down the blessing against flight and draws to himself the increase of blessing and its endurance through the ages; while the ignorant, by ingratitude and by what bequeaths the passing away of beneficence, and by committing what brings about affliction with cares and sorrows, is contrary to that. And it is possible that these too are among the repetitions; and from what we have mentioned the distinction appears on some of the aspects. And al-qawam, on the pattern of sahab, is justice and that by which one lives — that is, the choosing of the mean in acquiring what he needs and the contenting himself with the measure of sufficiency. And vying for more is contending in abundance — that is, acquiring the goods of this world beyond the measure of need, for vainglory and contention. And it is possible that what is meant is the mean in spending and the leaving of miserliness and prodigality, as He, exalted be He, said: "And those who, when they spend, are neither prodigal nor niggardly, but between that is a just balance" (1). So what is meant by vying for more is contending in the abundance of spending. And wisdom is acting by knowledge and choosing the more beneficial and fitting; and its opposite is following the caprice of the soul. And dignity is weight, gravity, firmness, not being disturbed by trials, and the leaving of frivolity and of rushing to what is not praised. The upshot is that the man of intellect does not depart from what he is upon by everything that comes upon him, and nothing moves him but what the intellect judges to be worth moving for or towards, out of regard for some good and benefit; while the ignorant is moved by fancies and imaginings and by following the appetitive and irascible powers. So the mover of the man of intellect is rare in occurrence, and the mover of the ignorant is much realized. And felicity is the choosing of what brings about a good end. And the seeking of forgiveness is more general than repentance, since in repentance the resolve to abandon in the future is a condition, and that is not a condition in the seeking of forgiveness; and it is possible that it is a confirmation of the preceding clause. And self-deception is being deceived by the soul and by Satan through the postponing of repentance and heedlessness of sins and of their harms and their punishments. And vigilance, that is, over the times of the prayers; and carelessness is the delaying beyond the times of excellence. Or what is meant is vigilance over

116.text: all the obligations. And disdaining is being proud; and God the Exalted has named the abandoning of supplication pride, saying: "Surely those who are too proud for My worship" (1). And gladness is the leaving of sorrow over what has escaped him of the world, or cheerfulness towards the brethren. His words "and fellowship, and its opposite separation" — in some copies it is "partisan zeal"; and its being the opposite of fellowship is because it entails dispute, obstinacy and stubbornness, which bring about the removal of fellowship. And the detailing of these qualities and their verification will come, if God the Exalted wills, in the chapters on noble character.

«8»- m', Ma'ani al-Akhbar: my father, from Muhammad al-'Attar, from al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad b. 'Abd al-Jabbar, from some of our companions, raising it to Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, who said: I said to him: What is the intellect? He said: That by which the Merciful is worshipped and by which the gardens are earned (2). He said: I said: Then what was that which was in Mu'awiya? He said: That is cunning, and that is devilry; and it is like the intellect, but it is not intellect.

sn, al-Mahasin: al-Ash'ari, the like of it. Elucidation: al-nakra' is shrewdness, acuteness and soundness of judgement; and when it is employed in the objects of desire of the hosts of ignorance it is called devilry, and for that reason he, peace be upon him, explained it by it. And this is either another power besides the intellect, or the intellectual power — and when it is employed in these false matters and is perfected in that, it is named devilry and is not named intellect in the usage of the sacred law. And its exposition has already passed.

«9»- m', Ma'ani al-Akhbar: al-Hasan b. 'Ali, peace be upon him, was asked, and it was said to him: What is the intellect? He said: The swallowing down of what chokes, until the opportunity is attained.

Elucidation: al-ghussa, with damma, is what lodges in the throat and is hard to swallow (3); and it is applied figuratively to the hardships that a man finds it hard to bear, and that is what is meant here. And the swallowing of it is a figure for the bearing of it and for not undertaking vengeance for it and the setting of it right until the opportunity is attained — for the setting of it right before that profits nothing but disgrace, the intensity of the trial and the abundance of care.

«10»- m', Ma'ani al-Akhbar, in the questions of the Commander of the Faithful to al-Hasan, peace be upon him: My son, what is the intellect? He said: Your heart's keeping of what is deposited with it. He said: Then what is ignorance? He said: Swiftness in leaping upon the opportunity before the mastery of it

Perhaps his defining the intellect, peace be upon him, by its properties and its concomitants rather than by setting out its reality and its quiddity is a pointer to the fact that knowledge and cognizance of its reality and its inmost nature is not possible. And the intellect here comprises the theoretical and the practical, because the worship of the Merciful and the earning of the gardens require the two together.
In one copy: and its swallowing is impossible.

117.text: and the withholding from answer. And an excellent help is silence in many situations, even if you are eloquent.

Elucidation: "what is deposited with it", in the passive construction — that is, what is placed with him as a deposit and whose keeping is asked of him. His words, peace be upon him, "and the withholding from answer" — that is, when there is no likelihood of harm in the answer; for withholding then is either from ignorance of it, or from ignorance of the interest of the moment, since the right course then is in the answer. So his words, peace be upon him, "and an excellent help", are like an exception from what precedes. And reports suited to this chapter will come in the chapter on the composition of man and his parts.

«11»- f, Tuhaf al-'Uqul: The Prophet — may God bless him and his family — said, in answer to Sham'un b. Lawi b. Yahuda, one of the disciples of Jesus, when he said: Tell me of the intellect — what it is, and how it is, and what branches from it and what does not; and describe to me all its classes. So the Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: The intellect is a tether (1) against ignorance. And the soul is like the most vicious of beasts: if it is not tethered it runs wild (2). So the intellect is a tether against ignorance. And God created the intellect and said to it: Come forward — and it came forward. And He said to it: Go back — and it went back. So God, blessed and exalted, said: By My might and My majesty, I have not created a creature greater than you nor more obedient than you. By you I begin and by you I restore; yours is the reward and upon you is the punishment. So there branched from the intellect forbearance; and from forbearance, knowledge; and from knowledge, right direction; and from right direction, chastity (3); and from chastity, self-guarding; and from self-guarding, modesty; and from modesty, gravity; and from gravity, perseverance in good; and from perseverance in good, hatred of evil; and from hatred of evil, obedience to the sincere counsellor. So these are ten classes of the kinds of good; and for each one of these ten classes there are ten kinds. As for forbearance, of it are: the pursuit of what is comely, the company of the righteous, a raising up from lowliness (4), a raising up from meanness, the desiring of good, its possessor's drawing near to the lofty degrees, pardon, and forbearing delay (5)
With kasra on the 'ayn: a rope with which the camel is bound at the middle of its foreleg.
With fatha on the 'ayn: restraint from what is not lawful or not seemly.
With kasra on the dad and with fatha: the lowering of the soul.
With fatha on the mim and quiescence of the ha' or its fatha: gentleness and deliberateness in action, and precedence in good. The first sense is what is meant here.

118.text: and kindness and silence (1). This is what branches for the man of intellect through his forbearance. As for knowledge, there branches from it sufficiency, though he be poor; and generosity, though he be miserly; and awe-inspiring dignity, though he be of no account; and safety, though he be sick; and nearness, though he be far off; and modesty, though he be boastful; and elevation, though he be lowly; and honour, though he be base; and wisdom, and favour. This is what branches for the man of intellect through his knowledge. So blessed is he who has intellect and knowledge. As for right direction, there branches from it soundness of judgement, guidance, piety, God-fearing, attainment, moderation, frugality, reward, nobility, and knowledge of God's religion. This is what the man of intellect attains through right direction. So blessed is he who thereby stands upon the highroad of the path. As for chastity, there branches from it contentment, humble submission, good fortune, rest, self-examination, humility, recollection, reflection, generosity and open-handedness. This is what branches for the man of intellect through his chastity — contentment with God and with His apportioning. As for self-guarding, there branches from it soundness, humility, scrupulousness, turning back to God, understanding, discipline, beneficence, the endearing of oneself, good, and the shunning of evil. This is what the man of intellect attains through self-guarding. So blessed is he whom his Master has honoured with self-guarding. As for modesty, there branches from it gentleness, compassion, watchfulness for God in secret and in the open, safety, the shunning of evil, cheerfulness, liberality (2), triumph, and fair praise of the man among people. This is what the man of intellect attains through modesty. So blessed is he who accepts God's counsel and fears His disgracing him. As for gravity, there branches from it kindliness, resolution, the rendering of the trust, the leaving of betrayal, truthfulness of tongue, the guarding of the private parts, the setting right of property, preparedness against the enemy, the forbidding of the reprehensible, and the leaving of foolishness. This is what the man of intellect attains through gravity. So blessed is he who is dignified, and who has no levity nor ignorance, and who pardons and overlooks. As for perseverance in good, there branches from it the leaving of enormities, distance from rashness (3)

With fatha on the sad and quiescence of the mim: keeping silent — that is, about what does not concern him and does not matter to him, and about what holds harm in it, whether by the sacred law or by reason.
With fatha on the undotted sin: generosity.
With fatha on the ta' and quiescence of the ya': recklessness and levity, and the departure of the intellect.

119.text: and scrupulous avoidance of sin, certainty, love of deliverance, obedience to the Merciful, the magnifying of the proof, the shunning of Satan, the answering of justice, and the speaking of truth. This is what the man of intellect attains through perseverance in good. So blessed is he who remembers what is before him, and remembers his standing, and takes a lesson from passing away. As for hatred of evil, there branches from it dignity, patience, victory, steadfastness upon the highroad, perseverance in right guidance, faith in God, abundance, sincerity, the leaving of what does not concern him, and vigilance over what benefits him. This is what the man of intellect attains through hatred of evil. So blessed is he who establishes the truth for God and holds fast to the handles of God's path. As for obedience to the sincere counsellor, there branches from it increase in intellect, completeness of understanding, praiseworthy outcomes, deliverance from blame, acceptance, love, illumination, equity, precedence in affairs, and strength for the obedience of God. So blessed is he who is safe from the places where caprice throws men down. So these qualities, all of them, branch from the intellect. Sham'un said: Then tell me of the marks of the ignorant (1). So the Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: If you keep his company he wearies you; if you withdraw from him he reviles you; if he gives you he reproaches you with it; if you give him he is ungrateful to you; if you confide in him he betrays you; if he confides in you he accuses you; if he becomes rich he grows insolent (2) and is coarse and harsh; if he becomes poor he denies God's blessing and is not scrupulous; if he rejoices he goes to excess and is overweening; if he grieves he despairs; if he laughs he brays; if he weeps he bellows. He falls upon the righteous, and does not love God nor watch for Him, nor is he ashamed before God nor does he remember Him. If you please him he praises you and ascribes to you of good what is not in you; and if he is displeased with you his praise departs and he ascribes to you of evil what is not in you. This is the course of the ignorant. He said: Then tell me of the mark of Islam. So the Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: Faith, knowledge and action. He said: Then what is the mark of faith, and what is the mark of knowledge, and what is the mark of action? So the Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: As for the mark of faith, it is four: the acknowledgement of God's oneness, faith in Him, faith in His books, and faith
Al-a'lam is the plural of 'alam, with fatha on the 'ayn and the lam: a thing set up by which one is guided. And the meaning is: tell me of the tokens of the ignorant and his marks.
Al-batar: overweening insolence at the coming of blessing.

120.text: in His messengers. As for the mark of knowledge, it is four: knowledge of God, knowledge of what He loves, knowledge of what He dislikes, and the keeping of them until they are rendered. As for action, it is prayer, fasting, alms and sincerity. He said: Then tell me of the mark of the truthful, and the mark of the believer, and the mark of the patient, and the mark of the repentant, and the mark of the grateful, and the mark of the humble, and the mark of the righteous, and the mark of the sincere counsellor, and the mark of the certain, and the mark of the sincere, and the mark of the abstinent, and the mark of the dutiful, and the mark of the God-fearing, and the mark of the affected, and the mark of the wrongdoer, and the mark of the ostentatious, and the mark of the hypocrite, and the mark of the envier, and the mark of the prodigal, and the mark of the heedless, and the mark of the slothful, and the mark of the great liar, and the mark of the transgressor, and the mark of the unjust. So the Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: As for the mark of the truthful, it is four: he is truthful in his speech; he holds true God's promise and His threat; he fulfils the covenant; and he shuns treachery. As for the mark of the believer, he is compassionate, and he understands, and he is modest. As for the mark of the patient, it is four: patience in the face of things disliked, resolve in the works of piety, humility, and forbearance. As for the mark of the repentant, it is four: sincerity to God in his work (1), the leaving of falsehood, cleaving to the truth, and eagerness for good. As for the mark of the grateful, it is four: gratitude in blessings, patience in affliction, contentment with God's apportioning, and that he praises and magnifies none but God. As for the mark of the humble, it is four: watchfulness for God in secret and in the open, the pursuit of what is comely, reflection upon the Day of Resurrection, and intimate converse with God. As for the mark of the righteous, it is four: he purifies his heart, and sets right his work, and sets right his earning, and sets right all his affairs. As for the mark of the sincere counsellor, it is four: he judges by the truth, and renders the truth from himself, and is content for people with what he is content with for himself, and transgresses against no one. As for the mark of the certain, it is six: he is certain that God is real, and so believes in Him; and he is certain that death is real, and so is wary of it; and he is certain that the raising is real, and so fears disgrace (2); and he is certain that the Garden is real, and so longs
That is, sincerity to God in his work.
In the abode of the hereafter, and on the day when the secrets are tried — so he does not do what brings about disgrace.

121.text: for it (1); and he is certain that the Fire is real, and so purifies (2) his striving for deliverance from it; and he is certain that the reckoning is real, and so calls himself to account. As for the mark of the sincere, it is four: his heart is sound (3), and his limbs are sound (4), and he expends his good and restrains his evil. As for the mark of the abstinent, it is ten: he abstains from forbidden things, and restrains himself, and performs the obligations of his Lord; so if he is owned he is excellent in obedience, and if he is an owner he is excellent in ownership; and he has neither partisan zeal nor rancour; he does good to whoever has done him evil, and benefits whoever has harmed him, and pardons whoever has wronged him, and humbles himself for God's right. As for the mark of the dutiful, it is ten: he loves in God, and hates in God, and keeps company in God, and parts in God, and grows angry in God, and is pleased in God, and works for God, and seeks from Him, and is humble before God — fearing, feared, pure, sincere, modest, watchful — and does good in God. As for the mark of the God-fearing, it is six: he fears God, and is wary of His seizing, and passes evening and morning as though he sees Him; the world does not trouble him (5), and nothing of it looms large for him, because of the goodness of his character (6). As for the mark of the affected, it is four: disputation about what does not concern him; and he contends with one above him; and he undertakes what he cannot attain (7). As for the mark of the wrongdoer, it is four: he wrongs the one above him (8) by disobedience, and possesses the one below him by domination, and hates the truth, and displays wrongdoing.
By the doing of good deeds and acts of piety, and by acquiring what brings about entrance into the gardens and distance from the fires.
From associating partners, from ostentation, from love of the world and its people, and its ornament and its show.
From acts of disobedience and from what holds their blight.
That is, the affair of the world does not grieve him nor disquiet him.
It appears that one of the six has dropped out.
"And he makes his concern what concerns him" — in Tuhaf.
Such as his Creator, his Prophet, his Imam, his teacher, his parents, and whoever's rights he is obliged to observe and whose sanctity he must guard.

122.text: As for the mark of the ostentatious, it is four: he is eager in working for God when someone is with him, and slothful when he is alone; and he is eager in all his affairs for praise; and he beautifies his outward bearing with all his effort. As for the mark of the hypocrite, it is four: his inward is corrupt; his tongue differs from his heart, and his speech from his deed, and his inner state from his outward. So woe to the hypocrite from the Fire. As for the mark of the envier, it is four: backbiting, fawning, and gloating at misfortune. As for the mark of the prodigal, it is four: boasting in falsehood; and he buys what is not his, and wears what is not his, and eats what he does not have. As for the mark of the heedless, it is four: blindness, inadvertence, diversion and forgetfulness. As for the mark of the slothful, it is four: he is slack until he falls short, and falls short until he squanders, and squanders until he sins and grows vexed. As for the mark of the great liar, it is four: if he speaks he does not speak truth, and if he is spoken to he does not believe; and talebearing, and calumny. As for the mark of the transgressor, it is four: diversion, idle talk, transgression and slander. As for the mark of the unjust, it is four: disobedience to the Merciful, the harming of neighbours, hatred of the Qur'an, and nearness to tyranny. So Sham'un said: You have healed me and given me sight after my blindness; so teach me paths by which I may be guided. So the Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — said: Sham'un, you have enemies who seek you and fight you to strip your religion from you, of the jinn and of mankind. As for those of mankind, they are a people who have no portion in the hereafter and no desire for what is with God; their whole concern is to reproach people for their deeds, while they do not reproach themselves nor beware of their own deeds. If they see you righteous they envy you and say: he is a show-off; and if they see you corrupt they say: there is no good in him. As for your enemies among the jinn, they are Iblis and his hosts. So when he comes to you and says: your son has died — say: the living were created only to die, and a piece (1) of me enters the Garden; that indeed gladdens. And when he comes to you and says: your wealth has gone — say: praise be to God, who gave and took, and has taken away from me the alms-due, so no alms-due is upon me. And when he comes to you and says: people wrong you while you do not wrong — say: the way is only on the Day
Al-bad'a, with kasra on the ba' and with fatha: the piece of flesh; and here it is a figure for the child.

123.text: of Resurrection against those who wrong people, "and against the doers of good there is no way". And when he comes to you and says to you: how great is your beneficence — wishing to bring you into self-admiration — say: my evildoing is more than my beneficence. And when he comes to you and says to you: how much is your prayer — say: my heedlessness is more than my prayer. And when he says to you: how much do you give to people — say: what I take is more than what I give. And when he says to you: how many there are who wrong you — say: those I have wronged are more. And when he comes to you and says to you: how much you do — say: long have I disobeyed. God, blessed and exalted, when He created the lowest, it boasted and swelled (1) and said: what thing can overcome me? So He created the earth and spread it out upon its back, and it was humbled. Then the earth boasted and said: what thing can overcome me? So God created the mountains and fixed them upon its back as pegs, lest it should sway (2) with them upon it; and the earth was humbled and settled. Then the mountains boasted over the earth and rose high (3) and stretched up and said: what thing can overcome me? So He created iron, and it cut them, and they were humbled. Then iron boasted over the mountains and said: what thing can overcome me? So He created fire, and it melted the iron, and iron was humbled. Then the fire roared (4) and blazed up (5) and boasted and said: what thing can overcome me? So He created water, and it quenched it, and it was humbled. Then water boasted and swelled and said: what thing can overcome me? So He created the wind, and it moved its waves and stirred up what was in its depths and held it back from its courses, and water was humbled. Then the wind boasted and blew hard and said: what thing can overcome me? So He created man, and he built and contrived what he might shelter behind from the wind and from other things, and the wind was humbled. Then man was overweening and said: who is stronger than I in power? So He created death, and it subdued him, and man was humbled. Then death boasted within itself; so God, Almighty and Glorious, said: do not boast, for I shall slaughter you (6) between the two parties, the people of the Garden and the people of the Fire, and then I shall never bring you to life again. So it feared. Then he said: And forbearance overcomes anger, and mercy overcomes displeasure, and charity overcomes fault.
That is, that it should move and be shaken.
That is, the sound of its kindling was heard.
Perhaps what is meant by its shahqa is the rising of its flames and its blaze.
Perhaps what is meant by the slaughtering of death is the annihilation of its causes.

124.text: Elucidation: His words, exalted be He, "by you I begin and by you I restore" — that is, by you I created creation and originated them, and by you I restore them for recompense; since but for the intellect obligation would not be fitting, and but for obligation there would be no benefit in creation, nor any profit in reward and punishment and the gathering, nor any wisdom in them.
