His words — may God bless him and his family — "and from forbearance, knowledge" — since by the abandoning of forbearance the learned shun him, so he cannot learn from them; and also God strips his knowledge from him and does not effuse wisdom upon him by his abandoning it, as will come. And right direction is being guided aright and standing firm upon the path of truth with steadfastness in it. And chastity is the restraining of the soul from forbidden things, and self-guarding is the restraining of it from doubtful and disapproved things; and for that reason it branches from chastity. And by self-guarding the coverings and the veils are lifted from the eye of the heart, so he sees the truth as truth and falsehood as falsehood, and so is ashamed to commit acts of disobedience. And when modesty is firmly established in him, gravity is attained for him — that is, not being disturbed by the appetitive and irascible movers, and not being shaken by trials; since modesty before his Lord prevents him from preferring anything to His good pleasure, or from leaving base matters in the service of his Master. And gravity becomes a means to perseverance in good things; and perseverance in good things entails God the Exalted's support that he should hate evils. So when he becomes a lover of good and a hater of evil, he obeys every sincere counsellor who guides him to the good he loves or restrains him from the evil he hates. As for what branches from forbearance, their branching from it becomes clear with the least reflection, and expanding the discourse upon them entails prolixity. And lowliness is with respect to the world, and meanness is what is by reason of blameworthy characters. And al-mahal, that is, the deferring of punishment and not hastening to vengeance.

As for what branches from knowledge: sufficiency, that is, sufficiency of soul, though he be poor without wealth; and sufficiency by wealth is also possible, though he was poor before knowledge. And generosity, that is, he is generous with realities to creation, though he be miserly in wealth, either for lack of it or from his miserliness; or what is meant is that knowledge becomes a cause of his generosity with wealth and with knowledge and with other things, though he was miserly before being qualified by knowledge. And awe-inspiring dignity is attained for him, though he be — with respect to what becomes a cause of it in the world — of no account, for lack of worldly honour, standing, lineage and wealth; yet by knowledge God casts his awe into the hearts of the servants, though he was before knowledge of no account and contemptible. And safety from faults, though he be sick in his body; or knowledge becomes a cause of his healing from bodily and spiritual sicknesses. And nearness to God, though he be far off — that is, distant from the noble

125.text: creation; or nearness to God and to creation, though he was far from both before knowledge. And modesty, though he be boastful. In al-Qamus: al-salaf, with the vowelling, is speaking with what your companion dislikes, and praising oneself for what one does not have; or exceeding the measure of refinement and claiming beyond that out of pride; and he is salif, on the pattern of katif — end of quotation. That is, there is attained from knowledge modesty in what is loved and praised, even if people count it boastfulness for his leaving off flattery; or, though he was before it boastful — and the latter here is the more evident. And elevation and honour also admit of the two senses, on the analogy of what has passed. And the distinction between them is that elevation is what belongs to himself, and honour is what passes over to another, in that whoever is ascribed to him is honoured on his account. And the first is with respect to worldly standing, and the second by spiritual elevation on account of noble characters. And wisdom is the sciences effused after acting by what one knows, or acting by knowledge, as will come. And favour is rank and nearness with God.

As for what branches from right direction: soundness of judgement, and it is what is correct in speech and in action. And guidance, that is, to what is above what he is in; or what is meant is that among its parts and its concomitants is guidance — and likewise piety and God-fearing. And attainment: perhaps what is meant by it is the degree by which the utmost of aims is attained, of nearness, of triumph and of felicity; for it is from attaining and hitting the mark. And moderation, that is, the middle straight path. And frugality is the observing of the praiseworthy mean in all matters and the leaving of excess and defect. And it is possible that what is meant by reward is the rewarding of another in recompense for what he does for him — but that is remote.

As for what branches from chastity: contentment with what God has given him of sustenance, and not dealing in the forbidden matter in seeking increase. And humble submission is lowliness and abasement, and it is among the concomitants of chastity, because whoever abstains from the forbidden and does not amass much wealth from it does not grow insolent, and abases himself and is humble. And good fortune is the portion — that is, the portions of the hereafter, since by leaving the portions of this world the portions of the hereafter are made abundant. And rest, that is, in this world and the next; since whoever amasses wealth in this world also has nothing but hardship and toil, and likewise whoever does not abstain from the forbidden in the matter of the private parts bears in this world hardships, disputes, the prescribed penalties of the law and other things. And self-examination: either what is meant is the examining of the states of the poor and the rendering of their rights, or the examining of the states of the soul and its faults — and the first is the more evident. And humility, since by the leaving of chastity humility in acts of worship is stripped away, as is known by experience. And recollection, that is, the recollection of death and of the states of the hereafter and of sins. And reflection, that is, upon the Origin and the Return, and upon what he was created for.

126.text: As for what branches from self-guarding: soundness — the soundness of his soul and his going out from corruptions and faults. And humility before the Creator and before created beings, and not being too proud to accept the truth. And scrupulousness is the shunning of forbidden and doubtful things. And turning back is repentance and returning to God the Exalted. And understanding is the understanding of the goodness and badness of things, and the understanding of the faults of the soul and the greatness of its Creator. And discipline is goodness of conduct in the service of the Creator and in associating with creation. And beneficence to another, and the earning of people's love, and the choosing of good and of what is better in its outcome, and the shunning of evil.

As for what branches from modesty: gentleness of manner and the absence of harshness; and compassion and mercy towards creation. And watchfulness — and it is what is between two persons, each of whom watches and observes his companion — that is, he knows in all his states and remembers that God is aware of him, so he is ashamed to disobey Him or to leave His obedience and turn to another; and he awaits at every moment His mercy and guards against the descent of His retribution. And safety from the afflictions that come upon man in this world and the next through the leaving of modesty; and likewise the shunning of evil. And triumph, and it is the reaching of the desire and the sought object. And people's fair praise of him.

As for what branches from gravity (1): kindliness and beneficence to creation, or gentleness and forbearing courtesy with them; or the doing of things with delicacy of management and with what he knows, after reflection, to be the way of reaching it, without haste and hurry. And resolution is the securing of a matter and the taking hold of it with assurance, and reflection upon the outcomes of affairs. And the guarding of the private parts, that is, the keeping of them and the preventing of them from the forbidden and the doubtful; and whoever has no gravity follows the appetites, and they move him at the first of the matter, so he falls into the forbidden and the doubtful without deliberation. And the setting right of property likewise is made possible only by gravity, since haste in affairs and the following of everything that occurs at first glance mostly entails loss. And likewise preparedness against the enemy is only by deliberateness and firmness. And likewise the forbidding of the reprehensible, for that too proceeds only by management and resolution. And al-taharruj is the straitening of the matter upon the soul, or the doing of what entails sin. He said in al-Nihaya: and among them is the tradition of the orphans, taharraju that they should eat with them — that is, they straitened it upon themselves; and so-and-so taharraja when he did an act by which he falls into harij, from al-haraj, which is sin and straitness — end of quotation. And upon the second it would be conjoined to rashness. And certainty,
With fatha on the undotted ra': dignity, stillness and firmness.

127.text: since by the abundance of acts of worship certainty is strengthened. And his words "obedience to the Merciful" — it is possible to conjoin it to deliverance; and were it conjoined to love, perhaps what is meant is its abundance and its increase, or that it is a fruit consequent upon perseverance in good — namely that he is obedient to the Merciful, and that suffices him as honour and excellence. And the proof is the argument and everything that entails the clarity of a matter. And the proofs of God the Exalted are His prophets and His proofs and His books, and the miracles of the prophets and the proofs, and the signs of the horizons and of the souls that indicate His existence, His greatness, His oneness and the rest of His attributes. And obedience and perseverance in it is a magnifying of those proofs and an acknowledgement of them; and disobedience is a belittling of them.

As for what branches from hatred of evil: dignity and the absence of wavering away from good; and patience in the face of things disliked in religion; and victory over the outward and inward enemies; and abundance, that is, in faith or in all acts of obedience; and the leaving of what does not concern him — that is, what does not matter to him nor benefit him.

As for what branches from obedience to the sincere counsellor: al-lubb is what is pure of everything, and perhaps what is meant here is the intellect pure of the mixture of appetites and caprices. And acceptance, that is, with the Creator and with creation; and likewise love. Or acceptance with God, and love among creation (1). And al-israj: perhaps what is meant is the lighting of the mind and the kindling of understanding. And it is possible that in the original it was al-inshirah — that is, the expansion of the breast and its broadening for the sciences — or al-istiraha, and it was miscopied to what you see. And precedence in affairs, that is, in good things. His words, peace be upon him, "from the places where caprice throws men down" — al-sar' is the casting upon the ground; and what is meant is the matters and situations in which the caprice of the soul throws down most of creation and overcomes them.

As for the marks of the ignorant: 'annaka, with doubling — that is, he wearied you, from al-'ana', which is fatigue and toil. "And if you give him he is ungrateful to you", without doubling — that is, he does not thank you. And al-fazz is the coarse of manner, the bad of character. And his words, peace be upon him, "he is not scrupulous" — that is, he does not straiten himself away from sin, ugliness and disobedience (2). "And if he laughs he brays" — that is, he opens his mouth and is filled with laughter. Al-Jazari said concerning it: "The most hateful of you to me are the babblers, the mouth-fillers" — they are those who expand in speech and open their mouths with it, taken from al-fahq, which is being filled and broadened. It is said: afhaqtu the vessel; fahiqa, yafhaqu, fahqan — end of quotation. "And if he weeps he bellows" — that is, he is anxious and cries out
Or the accepting of the counsel of the sincere counsellor.

128.text: like the beasts. Al-Jazari said: al-khuwar is the sound of cattle; and from it is the tradition of the slaying of Ubayy b. Khalaf: "so he fell bellowing as the bull bellows" — end of quotation. The upshot is that his joy and his anxiety are outside the mean. His words "he falls upon the righteous" — that is, he finds fault with them and blames them. His words — may God bless him and his family — "and he ascribes to you" — perhaps it is with doubling, that is, he sets down, from al-tawqi', which is what is set down in books and decrees; or without doubling, with the ba' understood, that is, he faults you with what is not in you. His words — may God bless him and his family — "and he holds true God's promise and His threat" — that is, he believes in the two of them and acts by what they require. "And he fulfils the covenant" — that is, his covenants with God and with creation. His words — may God bless him and his family — "so he purifies his striving" — that is, from ostentation, from self-admiration and from the rest of what spoils the deed. His words — may God bless him and his family — "his heart is sound" — that is, from ostentation, from the kinds of associating partners, and from blameworthy characters; and his limbs from acts of disobedience and from what shows the absence of sincerity in him. His words — may God bless him and his family — "he has no mahmiya" — a verbal noun from al-himaya, that is, the protecting of the people of falsehood; and it is close to the sense of al-hamiyya, which is partisan zeal and disdain. His words — may God bless him and his family — "and nothing looms large" — that is, the goodness of his character and his patience makes the hardships of the world easy for him. His words — may God bless him and his family — "he contends with one above him" — such as his Maker, exalted be He, and His Prophet, and his Imam, and his teacher, and his parents, and everyone whose obedience is incumbent upon him. "And he undertakes" — that is, he ventures upon and turns to the acquiring of a matter he cannot reach. His words — may God bless him and his family — "and he beautifies his outward bearing" (1) — al-samt is the bearing of the people of good; that is, he adorns his outward and likens himself to the people of righteousness to the utmost of his effort and his striving. His words — may God bless him and his family — "his inward is corrupt" — that is, the hidden parts of his affairs and the inward of his states are corrupt and depraved. Al-Firuzabadi said: a man's dakhl, with fatha and with kasra, is his house, his way, all his affair, his skin and his inner lining — end of quotation. His words — may God bless him and his family — "and as for the mark of the envier" — it appears that one of the four has dropped out from the copyists, as the like of it occurred earlier (2); or in place of "four" it was "three", as in the testaments of Luqman, where he said: the envier has three marks — he backbites when absent, and fawns when present, and gloats at misfortune. His words — may God bless him and his family — "he is slack" — that is, he slackens and falls short and does not concern himself with it. His words — may God bless him and his family — "they have no portion" — al-khalaq, with fatha, is the share and the portion. His words — may God bless him and his family — "and it indeed gladdens" — perhaps what is meant is that his entering the Garden passes over to me, so that I too enter on his account; so it would be a verb. And it is possible that it is a verbal noun — that is, that this is a cause of ease and of the facilitating of my affairs in the hereafter
With fatha on the undotted sin and quiescence of the mim.
In the mark of the God-fearing.

129.text: And it is possible that yasri is a verb, from their saying suriya 'anhu al-hamm — that is, the care was lifted; that is, this reflection becomes a cause of care being lifted from you (1). Then know that in the source from which it was transmitted there were, after his words "long have I disobeyed", defective clauses with much blank space between them, which we have omitted. And what is at the end of the report is perhaps a representation to set out that everything other than Him, exalted be He, is overcome and subdued by what is above it, and God is the Overcomer of everything. And the discussion of it will come in the Book of the Heaven and the World. And we have been brief in the exposition of this report only because the full treatment of it could not be accomplished save in a separate book devoted to that; and our earlier undertaking holds back the rein of the pen from prolixity.

«12»- f, Tuhaf al-'Uqul: The Prophet — may God bless him and his family — said: The description of the man of intellect is that he is forbearing towards whoever behaves ignorantly towards him (2); and he passes over whoever wrongs him; and he humbles himself before one below him; and he vies with one above him in the seeking of piety. And when he wishes to speak he considers: if it is good he speaks and gains; and if it is evil he keeps silent and is safe. And when a trial presents itself to him he seeks protection in God and holds back his hand and his tongue. And when he sees a virtue he seizes the chance of it. Modesty does not part from him, and greed does not appear from him. These are ten qualities by which the man of intellect is known. And the description of the ignorant is that he wrongs whoever mixes with him, and transgresses against one below him, and overbears one above him. His speech is without consideration: if he speaks he sins, and if he keeps silent he is inadvertent. And if a trial presents itself to him he hastens to it and it destroys him. And if he sees a virtue he turns away and is slow towards it. He does not fear his old sins, nor does he hold back, in what remains of his life, from sins. He is slack towards piety (3) and slow towards it, unconcerned with what has escaped him of that or with what he has squandered. These are ten qualities of the description of the ignorant, who has been deprived of the intellect.

Elucidation: al-Jazari said: al-nuhza is the opportunity, and intahaztuha — I seized it as a prize; that is, when he sees a virtue he seizes the opportunity with this virtue and does not delay it. His words, peace be upon him, "and if he keeps silent he is inadvertent" — that is, his silence is not out of regard for some good, but because he was inadvertent of speech. And al-rada is destruction; fa-ardathu — that is, it destroyed him. And it is said: ma aktarithu lahu — that is, I do not care about it.
And it is possible that it is a miscopying of yasurruni.
Jahila 'alayhi — that is, he behaved foolishly towards him.
In one copy: he is slack towards good.

130.text: «13»- sn, al-Mahasin: al-'Awsi, from Abu Ja'far al-Jawhari (1), from Ibrahim b. Muhammad al-Kufi, raising it, said: al-Hasan b. 'Ali, peace be upon him, was asked about the intellect. He said: The swallowing down of what chokes, and the humouring of enemies.
dh, Rawdat al-Wa'izin: from the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, the like of it; and he added in it: and forbearing courtesy with friends (2).
Elucidation: al-mudahana is the showing of other than what you conceal, and it is close to the sense of al-mudarat.

«14»- sn, al-Mahasin: some of our companions, raising it, said: He, peace be upon him, said: The man of intellect does not speak to one whose disbelieving him he fears, and does not ask of one whose refusal he fears, and does not proceed upon what he fears having to excuse himself for, and does not hope in one in whose being hoped in there is no trust.

«15»- sn, al-Mahasin: some of our companions, raising it, said: Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, said: A man's letter is taken as an indication of his intellect and of the place of his insight; and his messenger, of his understanding and his acuteness.

«16»- ms, Misbah al-Shari'a: al-Sadiq, peace be upon him, said: The man of intellect is he who is submissive in the answering of the truth, equitable in his speech; refractory before falsehood, contentious in his speech. He leaves his world and does not leave his religion. And the indication of the man of intellect is two things: truthfulness of speech and rightness of action. And the man of intellect does not speak of what the intellect denies, and does not expose himself to accusation, and does not leave off forbearing courtesy with whoever he is afflicted with. And knowledge is his guide in his deeds, and forbearance his companion in his states, and knowing helps him in his ways. And caprice is the enemy of the intellect, the opposer of truth and the consort of falsehood. And the strength of caprice is from appetite; and the root of the marks of appetite is the eating of the forbidden, heedlessness of the obligations, the making light of the practices, and the plunging into diversions.

Clarification: Al-Firuzabadi said: jamaha the horse, on the pattern of mana'a — jamhan, jumuhan and jimahan — and it is jamuh: it carried away its rider and overcame him. And he said: a man is khasim, on the pattern of fariha: a disputant. His words "whoever he is afflicted with" — that is, with associating and mixing with him. And istahana bi-l-shay' — that is, he despised it and lowered it. And the plunging into diversions is the entering into them and the rushing into them without deliberation, and the persisting in them.
In one copy: Abu Hafs al-Jawhari.

Al-Saduq set it down in his Amali, p. 398, by his chain from his father, from Ahmad b. Idris, from Muhammad b. Ahmad b. Yahya b. 'Imran al-Ash'ari, from Ahmad b. Abi 'Abd Allah, from 'Ali b. Ja'far al-Jawhari, from Ibrahim b. 'Abd Allah al-Kufi, from Abu Sa'id 'Uqaysa, who said: al-Hasan b. 'Ali b. Abi Talib, peace be upon him, was asked. And at p. 270, by his chain from Muhammad b. al-Hasan b. al-Walid, from al-Saffar, from Ibrahim b. Hashim, from 'Ali b. Ma'bad, from al-Husayn b. Khalid, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida, peace be upon him; and he added at the end of it: "and forbearing courtesy with friends".

131.text: «17»- dh, Rawdat al-Wa'izin; ghw, Ghawali al-La'ali: from the Prophet — may God bless him and his family — who said: The head of intellect, after faith, is affection towards people. And he — may God bless him and his family — said: The most intelligent of people is a doer of good who fears, and the most ignorant of them is an evildoer who feels secure.
«18»- dh, Rawdat al-Wa'izin: from the Prophet — may God bless him and his family — who said: The head of intellect, after faith in God, is the endearing of oneself to people.

«19»- dh, Rawdat al-Wa'izin: The Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, said: It is not for the man of intellect to be setting out save for three: the mending of a livelihood, or a favour in the hereafter, or a pleasure in what is not forbidden.

«20»- dh, Rawdat al-Wa'izin: It is related that the Prophet — may God bless him and his family — was asked: What is the intellect? He said: Acting in obedience to God; and those who act in obedience to God are the people of intellect.

«21»- And it is related that the Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — passed by a madman and said: What is with him? It was said: He is mad. So he said: Rather he is afflicted. The madman is only he who prefers this world to the hereafter (1).

«22»- dh, Rawdat al-Wa'izin: It is related from the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, from the Prophet — may God bless him and his family — that he said: It behoves the man of intellect, when he is a man of intellect, to have four hours of the day: an hour in which he converses secretly with his Lord; an hour in which he calls himself to account; an hour in which he comes to the people of knowledge, who aid him in the affair of his religion and counsel him; and an hour in which he leaves his soul to its pleasure of the affair of this world, in what is lawful and praiseworthy.

«23»- khts, al-Ikhtisas: al-Sadiq, peace be upon him, said: The most excellent of the natures of the intellect is worship; and the most reliable of its discourse is knowledge; and the most abundant of its portions is wisdom; and the most excellent of its stores is good deeds.
«24»- And he, peace be upon him, said: The completeness of the intellect is in three: humility before God, goodness of certainty, and silence except from good.
«25»- And he said: Ignorance is in three: pride, intensity of wrangling, and ignorance of God. Those are the losers.
«26»- And he, peace be upon him, said: A man's intellect increases after forty, to fifty and sixty; then his intellect diminishes after that.

«27»- And he said: When you wish to test a man's intellect in a single sitting, speak to him in the course of your speech of what cannot be. If he denies it, he is a man of intellect; and if he holds it true, he is a fool.
That is, he chose this world and preferred it to the hereafter.

132.text: «28»- And he, peace be upon him, said: The man of intellect is not stung from the same hole twice.

«29»- f, Tuhaf al-'Uqul: The testament of Musa b. Ja'far, peace be upon them both, to Hisham b. al-Hakam, and his description of the intellect. He, peace be upon him, said: Hisham, God, blessed and exalted, gave good tidings to the people of intellect and understanding in His Book, saying: "So give good tidings to My servants who listen to the word and follow the best of it; those are they whom God has guided, and those are the possessors of understanding" (1).

Elucidation: what is meant by "the word" is either the Qur'an or admonitions in general. "And follow the best of it" — that is, when they hesitate between two matters of it which cannot be combined, they choose the better of the two. And upon the first it is possible that what is meant by "the best" is the unambiguous verses. And it is possible to construe "the word" as speech in general, since there is no true saying but that it has a false opposite; so when he hears them he chooses the true of the two. And upon the supposition that what is meant by "the word" is the Qur'an or admonitions in general, it is possible to refer the pronoun to the verbal noun implied within — that is, they follow it with the best following.

Hisham b. al-Hakam, God, majestic and mighty, completed for people the proofs by the intellects, and conveyed to them the exposition, and indicated to them His lordship by the evidences. So He said: "And your God is one God; there is no god but He, the All-Merciful, the All-Compassionate. Surely in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, and the ships that run in the sea with what profits men, and the water God sends down from heaven wherewith He revives the earth after its death and scatters abroad in it all manner of beast, and the turning about of the winds and the clouds compelled between heaven and earth — surely there are signs for a people who understand" (2).

Elucidation: what is meant by the proofs is the demonstrations, or the prophets and the legatees, peace be upon them, and the arguing and the cutting off of excuse — that is, He completed His proof against people by what He gave them of intellects. And afda ilayhi — that is, he reached; and the ba' is for transitivity — that is, after He completed their intellect He cast to them the exposition of what it is incumbent upon them to know and to recognize. And in al-Kafi: "and He aided the prophets by the exposition". And the evidences are what He set out in His Book of the indications of lordship and of oneness; or what He made manifest of the traces of His making and His power in the horizons and in their own souls — and the first is more fitting for the inference. And "the alternation of night and day" — that is, their succeeding one another upon this observed order, in that one of them goes and the other comes

133.text: behind it. And by that His words, exalted be He, are explained: "He it is who made the night and the day a succession" (1). Or their differing in light and in darkness; or in increase and decrease and the entering of one into the other; or in length and shortness according to latitude; or the difference of each hour of their hours with respect to different places — so whatever hour is supposed, it is morning for one place and noon for another, and so on. And al-fulk comes as singular and as plural, and it is the ship. And ma in His words, exalted be He, "with what profits men", is either verbal-noun-forming — that is, with their profiting — or relative — that is, with that which profits them of things carried and things brought. And "the water God sends down from heaven": the first min is for beginning and the second is explicative; and "heaven" admits of the celestial sphere, the cloud, and the direction of height. And the reviving of the earth is by plants, blossoms and fruits. And "and scatters abroad in it" is conjoined to "sends down" or to "revives"; for beasts grow by fertility and live by rain. And al-bath is spreading and dispersing. And what is meant by the turning about of the winds is either their turning about in the quarters from which they blow — east, west, south and north; or in their states — hot and cold, stormy and gentle, barren and fertilizing; or His making them at one time for mercy and at another for punishment. And "the clouds compelled" — that is, they neither descend nor disperse, though nature requires one of the two, until God's command comes. And it is said: compelled to the winds, which turn it about in the air by the will of God the Exalted. And in the verse is an indication of the necessity of looking into the properties of the things He has made, exalted be He, and of inferring from them His existence, His oneness, His knowledge, His power, His wisdom and the rest of His attributes; and of the permissibility of taking to the sea, of trade and of journeys, for the fetching of foodstuffs and goods.

Hisham, God, majestic and mighty, has made an indication to the knowledge of Him — that they have a Governor. So He said: "And He has made subject to you the night and the day, and the sun and the moon; and the stars are made subject by His command. Surely in that are signs for a people who understand" (2). And He said: "Ha Mim. By the Book that makes clear — We have made it an Arabic Qur'an, that perhaps you may understand" (3). And He said: "And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning, for fear and for hope, and sends down water from heaven and revives with it the earth after its death. Surely in that are signs for a people who understand" (4).

Elucidation: in al-Kafi, "God has made that an indication" — that is, each of the signs mentioned before or after. And His words, exalted be He, "and He has made subject to you" — that is, He prepared them for your benefits. And "made subject", in the accusative, is a circumstantial expression of the whole — that is, He benefited you by them while they are made subject to God, who created them and governed them as He willed. And there read

134.text: Hafs "and the stars are made subject" as subject and predicate, so it is a generalizing of the ruling after its particularization. And Ibn 'Amir put the sun and the moon in the nominative also. And His words, exalted be He, "He shows you" — the verb is construed as a verbal noun with an implied an, or as an adjective of something omitted, that is, a sign by which He shows you the lightning; "for fear" — of the thunderbolt, or of the destruction of dwellings and crops, or of travelling; "and for hope" — that is, in rain and vegetation and the watering of crops, or for the one who stays at home. And their accusative is for causation of a verb entailed by the mentioned verb, since His showing them entails their seeing; or of the mentioned verb with an annexed noun implied, that is, a showing of fear and of hope; or by construing fear and hope as frightening and giving hope; or as a circumstantial expression, like "I spoke to him orally".

Hisham, then He admonished the people of intellect and made them desire the hereafter, saying: "And the life of this world is only play and diversion; and the abode of the hereafter is better for those who are God-fearing. Will you not understand?" (1) And He said: "And whatever thing you have been given is the enjoyment of the life of this world and its adornment; and what is with God is better and more lasting. Will you not understand?" (2)

Elucidation: "and the life of this world" — that is, its deeds — "is only play and diversion" that diverts people and occupies them away from what yields a lasting benefit. And al-mata' is what is enjoyed.
Hisham, then He made those who do not understand fear His punishment, saying: "Then We destroyed the others; and you pass by them in the morning and by night. Will you not understand?" (3)

Elucidation: his words, peace be upon him, "His punishment" — either the object of his words "made fear", or of "understand", or of both by contention. And al-tadmir is destruction — that is, after We delivered Lot and his family We destroyed his people. "And you", people of Mecca, "pass by" their dwellings in your journeys of trade to Syria, for Sodom (4) is on the way. "In the morning" — that is, entering upon morning — "and by night" — that is, and in the evening; or by day and by night. Is there not in you an intellect by which you may take a lesson?

Hisham, then He set out that the intellect is with knowledge, saying: "And these parables We strike for people, and none understands them but those who know" (5). Hisham, then He blamed those who do not understand, saying: "And when it is said to them: follow what God has sent down — they say: nay, we follow what we found our fathers upon. What, even though their fathers understood nothing and were not rightly guided?" (6) And He, exalted be He, said:
With fatha on the undotted sin: the village of the people of Lot.

135.text: "Surely the worst of beasts with God are the deaf, the dumb, who do not understand" (1). And He said: "And if you ask them: who created the heavens and the earth? — they will surely say: God. Say: praise be to God. Nay, most of them do not understand" (2). Then He blamed the many, saying: "And if you obey most of those on earth, they will lead you astray from the way of God" (3). And He said: "Most people do not know", and "most of them do not perceive".

Elucidation: "we found" — that is, we came upon. His words, exalted be He, "what, even though" — the waw is for circumstance or for conjunction, and the hamza is for rejection and wonder; and the answer to law is omitted — that is, if their fathers were ignorant, not reflecting upon the matter of religion nor rightly guided, would they still follow them? "Surely the worst of beasts" — that is, the worst of what creeps upon the earth, or the worst of the beasts; "the deaf" — from the hearing of the truth and its acceptance; "the dumb" — from the speaking of it. And his words "nay, most of them do not understand" is not in our Qur'an; and this verse is in Surat Luqman, and in it is "nay, most of them do not know". And perhaps it was so in their Qur'an (4). And likewise "and most of them do not perceive" is not in this Qur'an. So either this is his own speech, peace be upon him, or he set down the purport of some of the verses. And the pronoun refers to the unbelievers of Quraysh; and they held that the creator of the heavens and the earth is God the Exalted, but they associated the idols with Him, exalted be He, in worship.

Hisham, then He praised the few, saying: "And few of My servants are grateful" (5). And He said: "and few are they" (6); "and none believed with him but a few" (7). Hisham, then He mentioned the possessors of understanding with the fairest mention and adorned them with the fairest adornment, saying: "He gives wisdom to whom He wills; and whoever is given wisdom has been given much good. And none takes heed but the possessors of understanding" (8). Hisham, God says: "Surely in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart" (9) — meaning the intellect.

This possibility from him, may God have mercy on him, rests upon holding that alteration occurred in the Qur'an, and we have set out its falsity in its place. Rather the truth is that this is from an error of the copyists or of the transmitter in recording it. And how could he, peace be upon him, argue by a verse which the one addressed has no way of obtaining, even supposing that alteration had occurred? T.

136.text: And He said: "And We gave Luqman wisdom" (1) — he said: understanding and intellect. Hisham, Luqman said to his son: Humble yourself before the truth and you will be the most intelligent of people. My son, this world is a deep sea in which a great multitude has drowned; so let your ship in it be the fear of God, and its body faith, and its sail trust, and its master the intellect, and its guide knowledge, and its rudder patience.

Elucidation: "before the truth" — that is, before God, by faith in Him and obedience to Him; or before every truth when it becomes clear to you, by accepting it. 'Alam, with fatha on the lam or with kasra. And in al-Kafi: "and its lading faith" — that is, what is loaded into it and with which it is filled. And al-shira', on the pattern of kitab, is the broad sheet above a timber which the wind strikes so that it drives the ship on. And al-qayyim is the manager of the affair of the ship. And al-dalil is the guide. And he said in al-Mughrib: al-sukkan is the tail of the ship, because by it it is upheld and settled.

Hisham, for everything there is an indication; and the indication of the man of intellect is reflection, and the indication of reflection is silence. And for everything there is a mount; and the mount of the man of intellect is humility. And it suffices you as ignorance that you ride upon what you have been forbidden.

Elucidation: in al-Kafi, "the intellect" stands in both places in place of "the man of intellect". And the indication of the intellect, or of the man of intellect, is reflection, for he reaches his object by thought. And upon the reading of al-Kafi it is possible that what is meant is that reflection indicates that the man is possessed of intellect; and likewise what follows admits of both. "And the mount of the man of intellect is humility" — that is, with humility he is strengthened for what his intellect indicates to him, and is supported by God in his deeds; and with pride and the absence of obedience to God his intellect weakens and he is unable for his deeds in affairs, like a man on foot unable to reach the object. And upon the reading "the intellect" it is more evident, as is not hidden.

Hisham, were there in your hand a walnut and people said it is a pearl, it would not profit you while you know that it is a walnut; and were there in your hand a pearl and people said it is a walnut, it would not harm you while you know that it is a pearl.
Elucidation: its upshot is not being deceived by people's praise nor boasting of their commendation.
Hisham, God did not send His prophets and His messengers to His servants save that they might understand from God. So the best of them in responding

137.text: is the best of them in knowledge of God; and the most knowing of them in the affair of God is the best of them in intellect; and the most intelligent of them is the highest of them in degree in this world and in the hereafter.

Elucidation: the plural pronoun in his words, peace be upon him, "that they might understand", refers to the servants — that is, He did not send them save that the servants might understand from God what they would not understand except by the prophets' and the messengers' making them understand, peace be upon them.

Hisham, there is no servant but that an angel takes him by the forelock; so he does not humble himself but that God raises him, and does not magnify himself but that God lowers him. Hisham, God has two proofs against people: an outward proof and an inward proof. As for the outward, they are the messengers and the prophets and the Imams, peace be upon them; and as for the inward, they are the intellects. Hisham, the man of intellect is he whom the lawful does not distract from his gratitude and whom the forbidden does not overcome in his patience. Hisham, whoever sets three things in mastery over three has, as it were, aided his caprice to the demolishing of his intellect: whoever darkens the light of his thought by the length of his hope, and effaces the choice things of his wisdom by the excess of his speech, and quenches the light of his taking-lesson by the appetites of his soul — he has, as it were, aided his caprice to the demolishing of his intellect. And whoever demolishes his intellect has corrupted for himself his religion and his world.

Elucidation: "light" is in the nominative (1), since azlama has not been seen as transitive; and its annexation to thought is either explicative or possessive. And the reason for that is that by the length of hope he turns to the world and its pleasures, so he is distracted from reflection. And al-tarif is the new, uncommon matter in which there is preciousness. And the effacing of the choice things by excess is either because when he occupies himself with excess he is distracted from wisdom during the time of speaking excess; or because, when people have heard excess from him, they pay no regard to his wisdom; or because when he occupies himself with it God effaces wisdom from his heart.
Hisham, how shall your deed grow pure with God while you have distracted your intellect from the affair of your Lord and obeyed your caprice against the mastery of your intellect?

Elucidation: al-zakat comes in the sense of growth and in the sense of purity, and here it admits of both. And al-amr is the counterpart of prohibition, or in the sense of the matter generally — that is, the affairs pertaining to Him, exalted be He.
Hisham, patience in solitude is a mark of the strength of the intellect. So whoever understands from God, blessed and exalted,
Rather it is in the accusative, as it is said: God darkened the night, that is, He made it dark; and his denial of azlama's being transitive is out of place.

138.text: withdraws from the people of this world and from those who desire it (1), and desires what is with his Lord; and He is his intimate in desolation, and his companion in solitude, and his sufficiency in want, and his strengthener without a clan.

Elucidation: "understands from God" — that is, there is attained for him knowledge of His essence, His attributes, His rulings and His laws; or God gives him the intellect; or he knows matters by a knowledge that goes back to God, in that he took it from His prophets and His proofs, either without intermediary, or his intellect reached a degree at which God effuses His sciences upon him without the teaching of a human being. "And his sufficiency" — that is, what makes him sufficient; or, just as the people of the world have their sufficiency by wealth, his sufficiency is by God and by His nearness and by intimate converse with Him. And al-'ayla is poverty. And in al-Kafi: "without a clan"; and it is the tribe and the nearest kin (2).

Hisham, creation was set up for the obedience of God; and there is no deliverance save by obedience; and obedience is by knowledge; and knowledge is by learning; and learning is made firm by the intellect. And there is no knowledge save from a godly scholar; and the knowing of the scholar is by the intellect.

Elucidation: in al-Kafi, "the truth was set up". And nusiba is either a verbal noun or a passive verb — that is, God set up creation, or the truth and the religion, by the sending of the messengers and the sending down of the books, so that He might be obeyed in His commands and His prohibitions. "And learning is made firm by the intellect" — that is, it grows strong and firmly established; or from al-i'tiqad in the sense of assent and acknowledgement. "And the knowing of the scholar" — and in al-Kafi, "and the knowing of the knowledge", that is, the knowledge of the scholar; and what is here is the more evident. And the purpose is that knowledge's need for the intellect is from two aspects: for the understanding of what the scholar casts, and for the knowing of the scholar from whom knowledge ought to be taken.
Hisham, little work from the man of intellect is accepted and multiplied; and much work from the people of caprice and of ignorance is rejected.
Hisham, the man of intellect was content with the lesser of this world along with wisdom, and was not content with the lesser of wisdom along with this world; and for that their trade profited.

Withdrawal from the people of this world, from those who desire it and are absorbed in its pleasures, and from whoever turns a man away from reaching his right direction and completing his felicity, is praiseworthy. But withdrawal from the people of religion and from the community of the Muslims, and from whoever by keeping his company one gains insight in the affair of religion and desire for what is with God of bliss — that is blameworthy both by the sacred law and by reason.
Al-raht, with fatha on the ra': a man's people and his tribe; a number gathered from three to ten, and there is no woman among them.

139.text: Elucidation: "with the lesser of this world" — that is, the little and the small of it, along with much wisdom; and he was not content with the little of wisdom along with much of this world.

Hisham, if what suffices you makes you sufficient, then the least of what is in this world suffices you; and if what suffices you does not make you sufficient, then nothing of this world will make you sufficient. Hisham, the people of intellect left the excess of this world — so how much more sins! And the leaving of this world is of the meritorious, and the leaving of sins is of the obligatory. Hisham, the people of intellect abstained from this world and desired the hereafter, because they knew that this world is a seeker and a thing sought. So whoever seeks the hereafter, this world seeks him until he takes in full his sustenance from it; and whoever seeks this world, the hereafter seeks him, and death comes to him and corrupts for him his world and his hereafter.

In al-Kafi: this world is a seeker and a thing sought, and the hereafter is a seeker and a thing sought. And this world is a seeker of the man, that what is with it of the apportioned sustenance may reach him; and a thing sought, which the greedy seeks in quest of increase. And the hereafter is a seeker, seeking him that his appointed term may reach him; and a thing sought, which the seeker of the felicities of the hereafter seeks by righteous deeds.

Hisham, whoever desires sufficiency without wealth, and rest of heart from envy, and safety in religion — let him beseech God in his asking that He perfect his intellect. For whoever understands is content with what suffices him; and whoever is content with what suffices him is made sufficient; and whoever is not content with what suffices him will never attain sufficiency. Hisham, God, majestic and mighty, related of a righteous people that they said: "Our Lord, do not make our hearts swerve after You have guided us, and grant us mercy from Your presence; surely You are the Bestower" (1) — when they knew that hearts swerve and return to their blindness and their ruin. Indeed, he has not feared God who has not understood from God; and whoever has not understood from God, his heart is not bound upon a firm knowledge which he beholds, nor does he find its reality in his heart. And no one is such save he whose speech confirms his deed and whose inward accords with his outward; because God does not indicate the hidden inward of the intellect save by an outward from it that speaks of it.
Elucidation: al-zaygh is inclining and turning aside from the truth. And "their ruin" — that is, their destruction and their going astray.

140.text: His words, peace be upon him, "he whose speech confirms his deed", in the form of the active participle — that is, he ought first to do what he commands, then to command another, so that his speech may be confirming of what he does. And it is possible to read it in the form of the passive participle. His words, peace be upon him, "because God" and so on — that is, the intellect is a matter hidden in man; its existence in a person is not known save by what appears upon the limbs of its traces and by the good acts arising from it. And it is possible that what is meant by the intellect is knowing.

Hisham, the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, used to say: There is nothing with which God has been worshipped more excellent than the intellect. And no man's intellect is complete until there are in him diverse qualities: unbelief and evil are safe from him, and right direction and good are hoped for from him; and the excess of his wealth is expended and the excess of his speech is withheld; and his portion of this world is bare sustenance; and he is not sated with knowledge all his days. Lowliness with God is more beloved to him than might with other than Him (1); and humility is more beloved to him than honour. He reckons much the little kindness from another and reckons little the much kindness from himself; and he sees all people as better than he, and himself as the worst of them in his own eyes. And that is the completeness of the matter.

Elucidation: "all his days" — that is, in the whole of his age and his life. "Lowliness is more beloved to him" — what is meant is worldly lowliness and might, or the lowliness of the soul and its might and self-exaltation. "And that is the completeness of the matter" — that is, every matter of the matters of religion is completed by it; or as though it were all the matters of religion, by way of hyperbole (2). And what is meant by unbelief is all its kinds, according to what will come of its explanation in its place, if God the Exalted wills.

Hisham, whoever's tongue is truthful, his deed grows pure; and whoever's intention is good, increase is given in his sustenance; and whoever's kindness to his brethren and his family is good, his life is lengthened.
Elucidation: "his intention" — that is, his resolve upon acts of piety and of good; or what is meant is sincerity in his good deeds.
Hisham, do not grant wisdom to the ignorant, for you would wrong it; and do not withhold it from its people, for you would wrong them

Perhaps what is meant is that the man of intellect, when he sees that going along with people and following their way brings about the raising of his standing and the greatness of his rank among them and his distance from the truth, and that taking hold of religion and travelling the path of truth brings about lowliness among them, chooses lowliness with people — while being mighty with God — over might among them and distance from Him, exalted be He. Or that the lowliness of his soul, by his taking its rein and restraining it from its desires, is more beloved to him than the might of his soul by letting loose its rein and by the fulfilling of its needs and its hopes.

And it appears that what is meant by it is the completeness of the soul's lowliness and its poverty, and that is the last of the degrees of faith and the completeness of a man's intellect, and by it his affair is completed, as has come expressly stated in some of the traditions.

141.text: Hisham, as they left wisdom for you, so leave this world for them.

Hisham, there is no religion for one who has no manliness, and no manliness for one who has no intellect. And the greatest of people in worth is he who does not reckon this world of any account for himself. Indeed, your bodies have no price save the Garden; so do not sell them for anything else.

Elucidation: al-muru'a is humanity and the completeness of manhood, and it is the quality comprising the noble characters and the fair proprieties. And al-khatar is the share, the portion, the worth, the rank, and the stake wagered upon; and all are possible.

Hisham, the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, used to say: None sits at the head of the gathering save a man in whom are three qualities: he answers when he is asked; he speaks when the people are unable to speak; and he counsels with the judgement in which is the good of its people. So whoever has nothing of them in him and yet sits, he is a fool. And al-Hasan b. 'Ali, peace be upon them both, said: When you seek your needs, seek them from their people. It was said: Son of the Messenger of God, and who are their people? He said: Those whom God recounted in His Book and mentioned, saying: "Only the possessors of understanding take heed." He said: they are the people of intellects. And 'Ali b. al-Husayn, peace be upon them both, said: Sitting with the righteous is a summoner to righteousness; and the discipline of the learned is an increase in intellect; and obedience to those charged with the intellect is the completeness of might; and the completing of wealth is the completeness of manliness; and the guiding of one who seeks counsel is a discharging of the due of the blessing; and the restraining of harm is of the completeness of the intellect, and in it is the body's rest, soon and late.

Elucidation: "the discipline of the learned is an increase in intellect" — that is, sitting with them and learning their proprieties and looking upon their acts and their characters entails an increase of intellect. And "the completing of wealth" — and in al-Kafi "the making of wealth fruitful", that is, the making it grow by trade and earnings — is an indication of the completeness of humanity and also entails it. His words "a discharging of the due of the blessing" — that is, thanks for his brother's due upon him, in that he made him the place of his counsel; or thanks for the blessing of the intellect, which is among the greatest of blessings — and perhaps the latter is the more evident.

Hisham, the man of intellect does not speak to one whose disbelieving him he fears; and does not ask of one whose refusal he fears; and does not promise what he has no power over; and does not hope for what he would be reproached for hoping; and does not go forward upon what he fears being unable for. And the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, used to counsel his companions, saying: I counsel you to fear of God in secret and in the open, and to justice in contentment and in anger, and to earning in poverty and in wealth, and that you join him who

142.text: has cut you off, and pardon him who has wronged you, and show tenderness to him who has deprived you. And let your looking be a taking-of-lesson, and your silence reflection, and your speech remembrance. And beware of miserliness, and take to open-handedness; for no miser enters the Garden, and no open-handed man enters the Fire.

Elucidation: al-ta'nif is blaming and reproaching with harshness and the leaving of gentleness, and both are possible. And secret and open are with respect to creation. And contentment and anger — that is, whether he is content with the one he deals justly with, or displeased with him. The upshot is that his contentment with someone or his displeasure with him should not become a cause of departing from the truth. And earning admits of the earning of this world and of the hereafter.

Hisham, God have mercy on him who is ashamed before God with the due of shame: so he guards the head and what it holds, and the belly and what it contains; and remembers death and decay; and knows that the Garden is hedged about with things disliked and the Fire is hedged about with appetites.

Elucidation: "and what it holds" — that is, what the head holds of the eye, the ear, the tongue and the rest of the perceptive faculties, in that he guards them from what is forbidden him. "And the belly and what it contains" — that is, what it gathers of food and drink, in that the two should not be from what is forbidden. And al-bila, with kasra, is wearing away and dissolving in the grave. He said in al-Nihaya, concerning it: "Being ashamed before God with the due of shame is that you do not forget the graves and decay, and the cavity and what it contains" — that is, what it gathers of food and drink, so that the two may be from what is lawful for them — end of quotation. And some of them said: al-jawf is the belly and the private parts, and they are the two cavities. And some of them related the report thus: "so let him guard the head and what it contains, and the belly and what it holds", and said: that is, what the head contains of the eye, the ear and the tongue — that is, he guards it from being employed in what does not please God, and from prostrating to other than God; and he guards the belly and what it holds, that is, what it gathers so that it is joined to it, of the private parts, the two feet, the two hands and the heart, from being employed in acts of disobedience — end of quotation. I say: so it is possible, upon what is in this report, that what is meant is the guarding of the belly from the forbidden, and the guarding of what the belly contains of the heart from corrupt beliefs and blameworthy characters. And it is possible that what is meant by what it contains is what it gathers and encompasses, of the two private parts and the rest of the limbs such as the two hands and the two feet; or that what is meant by the belly is what is other than the head, figuratively, by the indication of the contrast. His words, peace be upon him, "and the Garden is hedged about with things disliked" — that is, it is not attained save by enduring things disliked in this world.

143.text: Hisham, whoever restrains himself from the honour of people, God will forgive him his stumbling on the Day of Resurrection; and whoever restrains his anger from people, God will restrain from him His anger on the Day of Resurrection.

Elucidation: al-'athra is the slip, and what is meant is acts of disobedience. And al-iqala is originally the annulling of a sale at the buyer's request, and al-istiqala is the seeking of that. And what is meant here is God's passing over and the leaving of the punishment which the servant earned by the evil of his deed — as though he had bought the punishment and then regretted and sought its annulment.

Hisham, the man of intellect does not lie, even if his caprice is in it. Hisham, there was found on the strap of the sword of the Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family: The most insolent of people towards God is he who strikes one who did not strike him, and slays one who did not slay him. And whoever takes as patrons other than his patrons has disbelieved in what God sent down upon His Prophet Muhammad — may God bless him and his family. And whoever brings about an innovation, or shelters one who brings about an innovation, God will not accept from him on the Day of Resurrection any turning-away or any ransom.

Elucidation: perhaps what is meant by dhu'abat al-sayf, with the hamza, is what is hung upon it for the keeping of necessities such as salt and other things. Al-Jawhari and al-Firuzabadi said: al-dhu'aba is the piece of leather hung upon the rear of the saddle. And a'ta is from al-'utuww, which is insolence, exceeding the truth, and pride. "One who did not slay him" — that is, one intending to slay him, or the slayer of the one he inherits from. "And whoever takes as patrons other than his patrons" — that is, the freedman who ascribes himself to other than his emancipator; or the man of lineage who disowns his lineage; or the patrons in religion from among the Imams of the believers, in that he makes another his patron and takes him as an Imam — and upon the last the reliable reports indicate. And al-hadath is innovation, or slaying as has come in the report, or every reprehensible matter. He said in al-Nihaya: and in the tradition of Medina, "whoever brings about in it a hadath or shelters a muhdith" — al-hadath is the newly arisen reprehensible matter which is not customary nor known in the sunna. And al-muhdith is related with kasra on the dal and with fatha, as active and as passive participle. So the sense of the kasra is one who aids a criminal and shelters him and protects him from his adversary and stands between him and his being retaliated against; and the fatha is the innovated matter itself, and the sense of sheltering in it would be contentment with it and forbearance towards it — for when he is content with the innovation and confirms its doer and does not disapprove of it, he has sheltered it.

And al-Firuzabadi said: al-sarf in the tradition is repentance and al-'adl is ransom; or al-sarf is the supererogatory and al-'adl the obligatory, or the reverse; or it is weight and al-'adl is measure; or it is earning and al-'adl is ransom, or stratagem.

144.text: I say: al-sarf has been explained in some of our reports as repentance and al-'adl as ransom, as will come.

Hisham, the most excellent thing by which the servant draws near to God, after the knowledge of Him, is prayer, and dutifulness to parents, and the leaving of envy, of self-admiration and of boasting.
Elucidation: it is possible to bring all the necessary beliefs into "the knowledge", especially with the absence of the adverbial phrase, as has come in many reports without it.

Hisham, the most fitting of your days is the one that is before you; so look what day it is and prepare for it the answer, for you will be halted and questioned. And take your admonition from time and its people, for time is long and short. And work as though you see the reward of your work, that you may be the more eager for that. And understand from God, and look into the turning of time and its states; for what is coming of this world is like what has passed away of it — so take a lesson from it. And 'Ali b. al-Husayn, peace be upon them both, said: All that the sun rises upon in the easts of the earth and its wests, its sea and its land, its plain and its mountain, is, with a friend among the friends of God and the people of the knowledge of God's due, like the shade of shadows. Then he said: Is there no free man who will leave this leaving-in-the-mouth to its people? — meaning this world. Your souls have no price save the Garden; so do not sell them for anything else. For whoever is content with this world from God has been content with the base.

Elucidation: the length of time in itself does not conflict with its shortness in relation to each person — that is, take your admonition from the ages past and the times gone by. And it is possible that it is the life of each person in two respects.

And al-Firuzabadi said: al-zill, with kasra, is the opposite of sunlight; or it is al-fay'; or it is in the morning and al-fay' in the evening; its plural is zilal and zulul (1) and azlal. And the zill of everything is its figure, or its covering (2). And of the cloud, what veils the sun of it. And al-zulla is what shades you of a tree; and al-zulla, with damma, is what one shelters under, and the plural is zulal and zilal. And he said: al-fay' is what was sunlight and the shade supersedes it. And al-Tibi said: al-zill is what the sun supersedes, and al-fay' is what supersedes the sun. I say: so it is possible that what is meant is among the things that have shadows, such as the tree, the wall and the like; or what is meant is the likening to al-fay', which is a kind of shadow — for al-fay', by its coming into being, is more like this world than the rest of shadows; or for what is in it
Zilal with kasra on the za'; zulul with damma on the za'.
With kasra on the kaf and doubling of the nun: the covering of a thing and its shelter.

145.text: of the suggestion of shifting, changing and moving — that is, the shifting, changing shadows. And al-Jawhari said: al-lumaza, with damma, is what remains in the mouth of food; and from it is the saying of the poet describing this world: a leaving-in-the-mouth of days, like the dreams of a sleeper. I say: the excellence of this likening is not hidden, since everything of this world that is made easy for you is a leaving-in-the-mouth of one who ate it before you, and another profited by it more than your profiting, and left its spoilt part for you.

Hisham, all people see the stars, but none is guided by them save one who knows their courses and their mansions. And likewise you study wisdom, but none of you is guided by it save one who acts by it.

Elucidation: since among the greatest benefits of the stars is the knowing of times and of the direction of the way in journeys and the like, and the knowledge of those matters is not completed save by much attending to the stars, so that their courses, their mansions, their risings, their settings and the measure of their motion may be known — likewise wisdom is not profited by save by much attending to it and employing it, so that its benefits and its effects may be known. And darasa, on the pattern of nasara and of daraba, is "he read".

Hisham, the Messiah, peace be upon him, said to the disciples: O evil servants, the height of the palm-tree appals you, and you remember its thorns (1) and the trouble of climbing it, and you forget the goodness of its fruit and its benefits. Likewise you remember the trouble of the work of the hereafter, so its term seems long to you, and you forget what you will come to of its bliss, its light and its fruit. O evil servants, clean the wheat and make it good and grind it fine, and you will find its taste and its eating will be wholesome to you. Likewise, make faith sincere and complete it, and you will find its sweetness and its outcome will profit you. Truly I say to you: were you to find a lamp burning with tar on a dark night, you would seek light by it, and the smell of its stench would not keep you from it. Likewise it behoves you to take wisdom from whomever you find it with, and let not the badness of his desire for it keep you from him. O servants of this world, truly I say to you: you will not attain the honour of the hereafter save by leaving what you love. So do not defer repentance to tomorrow, for before tomorrow is a day and a night, and God's decree in them comes at morning and at evening. Truly I say to you: he who has no debt to people is more at rest and less in care than he who has debt upon him, even if he repays it well. And likewise he who has not done the fault is more at rest and less in care than he who has done the fault, even if he makes his repentance sincere and turns back. And the small of sins and the belittled of them are among the wiles of Iblis: he belittles them for you and makes them small
With fatha on the shin and quiescence of the waw: what comes out of a plant resembling needles.

146.text: in your eyes, so they gather and become many and encompass you. Truly I say to you: people in respect of wisdom are two men. A man who has made it firm by his speech and confirmed it by his deed; and a man who has made it firm by his speech and squandered it by the badness of his deed. And how far apart are the two! So blessed (1) are the learned in deed, and woe (2) to the learned in speech. O evil servants, take the mosques of your Lord as prisons for your bodies and your brows; and make your hearts houses for God-fearing, and do not make your hearts a refuge for appetites. The most anxious of you at affliction is the strongest of you in love of this world; and the most patient of you in affliction is the most abstinent of you in this world. O evil servants, do not be like the snatching kites, nor like the deceiving foxes, nor like the treacherous wolves, nor like the insolent lions. As they do with their prey, so you do with people: a party you snatch, and a party you deceive, and a party you overpower. Truly I say to you: it does not avail the body that its outward be sound and its inward corrupt. Likewise your bodies, which have pleased you, do not avail while your hearts are corrupt. And what avails you that you cleanse your skins while your hearts are filthy? Do not be like the sieve, from which the good flour comes out while it holds back the bran. Likewise you bring wisdom out of your mouths while rancour (3) remains in your breasts. O servants of this world, your likeness is only the likeness of the lamp: it gives light to people and burns itself. O Children of Israel, press close to the learned in their gatherings, even upon your knees; for God revives dead hearts by the light of wisdom as He revives the dead earth by the heavy rain.

Elucidation: 'abid al-saw', with fatha — and the sin is sometimes given damma, though some have forbidden the damma — and it is of the sort of the annexation of the qualified to the quality, like their saying hatim al-jud. And "the trouble of climbing it" — that is, the hardship of ascending it. And "its benefits", from al-rifq in the sense of kindness and profit; and perhaps it was marafiquha in the plural form, and the pronoun refers to the fruit or to the palm-tree. His words "what you will come to" — from their saying afda ilayhi, that is, he reached. And "its light", with damma on the nun and with fatha. And al-qamh, with fatha, is wheat. And yahna'ukum, with hamza, with fatha on
Al-tuba: gladness and felicity; good and the best. It is of the fu'la form from al-tib, the ya' being turned to waw for the damma before it. It is said: tuba laka and tubaka in annexation.
Al-wayl: the descent of evil, destruction; and it is invoked upon one who has fallen into a destruction he deserves.
Al-ghill, with kasra on the ghayn: rancour and deceit.

147.text: the nun and with kasra — that is, its eating is not followed by harm. And the ghibb of everything, with kasra, is its outcome. And al-qatiran, with fatha on the qaf and with kasra and quiescence of the ta', and with fatha on the qaf and kasra on the ta', is a stinking oil drawn from the abhal tree, with which mangy camels are anointed (1) (2), and fire is quickly kindled in it. And "the badness of his desire for it" — that is, his leaving off acting by that wisdom. And al-inzar is deferring; and perhaps its being made transitive by the ba' is by implication or by an implied word, and its being redundant is possible. And his words "comes at morning" — that is, it descends at the first of the day; "and at evening" — that is, it descends at the end of the day. And his words "more at rest" — that is, more in rest. His words "and the belittled of them", with fatha on the mim, the qaf and the ra' and quiescence of the ha', a verbal noun in the sense of lowliness and abasement; or on the pattern of the passive participle of the second form, as has come: "beware of the belittled of sins". And yuhaqqiruha is of the second form, or on the pattern of yadribu. And al-hida', with kasra on the ha' and lengthened, is the plural of hida'a, on the pattern of 'inaba, a kind of crow (3) that snatches things. And al-usud, with damma on the hamza and quiescence of the sin, is the plural of asad. And al-'atiya — that is, the wronging, the overweening, the proud. "As they do" — that is, the lions, or all that has preceded; so al-fara'is is by predominance. And his words "a party you snatch", to the end of what is mentioned, is by way of wrapping and unfolding; and since he mentioned the tearing of prey first, he did not mention it last. "It does not avail the body" — that is, it does not profit it nor repel from it an evil. And al-munkhul, with damma on the mim and the kha' — and its kha' is sometimes given fatha — is what one sifts with. And it is said zahamahum — that is, he pressed upon them and entered into their crowding. Al-Firuzabadi said: jatha, on the pattern of da'a and of rama, juthuwwan and juthiyyan with damma on the two, is he sat upon his knees; and jathaytu my knee to his knee. And he said: al-wabil is the heavy rain, great of drop.

Hisham, it is written in the Gospel: Blessed are the merciful to one another, they are the ones shown mercy on the Day of Resurrection. Blessed are the makers of peace between people, they are the ones brought near on the Day of Resurrection. Blessed are those whose hearts are purified, they are the God-fearing on the Day of Resurrection. Blessed are the humble in this world, they will ascend the pulpits of kingship on the Day of Resurrection.
Elucidation: the specifying of their being of the God-fearing to the Day of Resurrection is because on that day the God-fearing
Hana'a the camels: he anointed them with al-hina', which is tar.
Al-jarab: a disease that produces in the skin small pustules with severe itching.
There is an error in this; rather it is of the birds of prey, of the hawk kind, not of the crow.

148.text: are truly made plain and are distinguished from the criminals and are gathered to the Merciful as a delegation. As for in this world, often others are made to resemble them.

Hisham, fewness of speech is a great wisdom; so take to silence, for it is a goodly ease, a lessening of burden and a lightening of sins. So fortify the door of forbearance, for its door is patience. And God, Almighty and Glorious, hates the great laugher without wonder and the great walker to no purpose. And it is incumbent upon the governor to be as the shepherd, not heedless of his flock nor proud over them. So be ashamed before God in your inward selves as you are ashamed before people in your outward. And know that the word of wisdom is the believer's lost thing; so take to knowledge before it is raised up — and its raising up is the absence of your scholar from among you.
Elucidation: al-hukm, with damma, is wisdom. And al-da'a, with fatha on the dal, is stillness and rest. And al-irb, with kasra and with the vowelling, is need. And he said in al-Nihaya:
And in the tradition: the word of wisdom is the believer's lost thing.
And in a narration: the lost thing of every wise man.

that is, he does not cease to seek it as a man seeks his lost thing — end of quotation. And it is said: what is meant is that the believer takes wisdom from everyone he finds it with, even if he be an unbeliever or a transgressor, just as the owner of a lost thing takes it wherever he finds it; and what has passed supports it. And it is said: what is meant is that whoever has with him a wisdom he does not understand and does not deserve must seek one who will take it by its due, just as the announcing of a lost thing is obligatory; and when he finds one who deserves it he must not be miserly in bestowing it, as with the lost thing.

And he said in al-Nihaya: in the tradition, "so they stayed bayna zahranayhim and bayna azhurihim" — this expression has recurred in the tradition, and what is meant by it is that they stayed among them by way of seeking support and leaning upon them. And an alif and a nun with fatha were added to it for emphasis. And its meaning is that a back of them is before him and a back behind him, so he is sheltered on his two sides and on his sides, when it is said bayna azhurihim; then it became common until it was used for staying among a people generally.

Hisham, learn of knowledge what you are ignorant of, and teach the ignorant of what you know. And magnify the scholar for his knowledge, and leave off contending with him; and belittle the ignorant for his ignorance, but do not drive him away — rather bring him near and teach him.
Hisham, every blessing you are unable to give thanks for is in the position of a misdeed for which you are called to account. And the Commander of the Faithful said

149.text: God's blessings be upon him: God has servants whose hearts the fear of Him has broken and whom it has silenced from speech, though they are eloquent, possessed of intellect. They race to God with pure deeds. They do not reckon much for Him the much, nor are they content for Him with little from themselves. They see themselves as the worst, though they are the shrewd (1) and the righteous.

Elucidation: perhaps what is meant by inability is the leaving of it, the making of the soul incapable, and sloth — not the absence of power. That is, God calls to account for the leaving of thanks for a blessing as He calls to account for the doing of a misdeed, even if in this world, by the passing away of the blessing. And al-istibaq is racing in a contest — that is, some of them outstrip others in drawing near to God by deeds pure of their blights, or growing. And al-kiyasa is intellect and acuteness.
Hisham, modesty is of faith, and faith is in the Garden; and foul speech is of coarseness, and coarseness is in the Fire.

Elucidation: al-badha', with fatha on the ba' and lengthened, is obscenity and every ugly speech. And al-jafa', lengthened, is the opposite of kindness and the joining of ties; and it is sometimes applied to remoteness from the proprieties. And al-Mutarrizi said: al-jafa' is coarseness in company, roughness in dealing, and the leaving of gentleness.

Hisham, speakers are three: one who profits, one who is safe, and one who perishes. As for the one who profits, he is the one who remembers God; and as for the one who is safe, he is the silent; and as for the one who perishes, he is the one who plunges into falsehood. God has forbidden the Garden to every obscene, foul-mouthed man of little modesty, who cares not what he says nor what is said of him. And Abu Dharr, may God be pleased with him, used to say: Seeker of knowledge, this tongue is a key of good and a key of evil; so set a seal upon your mouth as you set a seal upon your gold and your silver (2).

Elucidation: what is meant by the speakers is those able to speak; or the speakers and those sitting with them, by predominance. The upshot is that people in the matter of speech are of three classes. And al-shajb is destruction, grief and fault. Al-Jazari said:
in the tradition of al-Hasan: gatherings are three — one safe, one gaining, and one perishing.
that is, perishing. It is said shajaba, yashjubu, so he is shajib; and shajiba, yashjabu, so he is shajib — that is, either safe from sin, or gaining reward, or perishing and sinning.
The plural of al-kayyis: the refined, the acute, the good in understanding and in discipline.
With the tripled waw and quiescence of the ra', and with fatha on the waw with kasra on the ra': minted dirhams.

150.text: Hisham, an evil servant is a servant who is two-faced and two-tongued: he lavishes praise on his brother when he sees him, and devours him (1) when he is absent from him. If he is given, he envies him; and if he is afflicted, he forsakes him. And the swiftest of good in reward is piety, and the swiftest of evil in punishment is insolence. And the worst of God's servants is he whose company is disliked for his obscenity. And does anything cast people upon their nostrils in the Fire but the harvests of their tongues? And of the goodness of a man's Islam is the leaving of what does not concern him.

Elucidation: al-itra' is exceeding the bound in praise and lying in it. And khadhalahu — that is, he left off aiding him. And al-baghy is transgression, overbearing, wrongdoing, and every exceeding of the bound. And his words "whose is disliked" is either with fatha on the ta' for the second person, or with damma in the passive construction.
